content: Elon Musk is known for having planet-sized ambitions, and his latest pronouncement lives up to that billing. "This will sound super crazy, but I see a path to SpaceX being worth orders of magnitude more than the current Earth economy," the Tesla and SpaceX CEO wrote in a Thursday post on X. The International Monetary Fund projected in April that the total value of world output, measured at market exchange rates, would hit $126 trillion this year. SpaceX had a $2.2 trillion market capitalization at Thursday's close, meaning the global economy is worth roughly 57 times more. Musk's vision of SpaceX becoming at least two orders of magnitude — 100 times — more valuable suggests it will one day have a market cap in excess of $12 quadrillion. All else being equal, SpaceX's stock price would have to rise 5,500-fold to achieve that valuation, meaning $1,000 invested today would skyrocket in value to $5.5 million. This will sound super crazy, but I see a path to SpaceX being worth orders of magnitude more than the current Earth economy Musk elaborated on his statement in a Friday post. "'Seeing a path' is not a statement of extreme confidence that we will achieve that outcome," he wrote. "Just means that I believe there is such a path and the probability of achieving it is not zero." SpaceX's revenue amounted to $7.8 billion in the second quarter, up 92% from the same period last year. The maker of rockets, spacecraft, and satellites recorded a $541 million net loss, down from $1 billion 12 months earlier. Musk told Wall Street analysts in August that SpaceX was internally projecting $1 trillion of revenue in 2030, and there was a "non-zero chance" it could reach that milestone in 2029. But even if the company hits that mark, then grows revenue 100-fold from there to $100 trillion, that would still be less than 1% of the minimum company valuation Musk envisions. "I guess his idea is that SpaceX will open up new colonies or human civilizations beyond the Earth, and thus tap into minerals, energy, and growth beyond what we are capable of with the finite resources we have available to us here," Russ Mould, AJ Bell's investment director, told Business Insider by email. Yet there are likely to be "considerable risks and obstacles" when it comes to operating in space or on other planets, he continued, "not to mention considerable expense." Those challenges mean that an investor using a discounted cash flow to value SpaceX today should apply an "extremely high" discount rate to those potential cash flows, Mould said, so the "theoretical value of SpaceX equity may not be as high as some might think." Ipek Ozkardeskaya, a senior analyst at Swissquote Bank, echoed Mould's point about SpaceX likely having to spend huge sums to travel to other planets and capitalize on their resources. "What he doesn't say is how much it will cost to get there!" she told Business Insider by email. Other analysts took a more measured view. "Musk is a believer and a stargazer!" Neil Wilson, investor strategist at Saxo UK, told Business Insider by email, adding that SpaceX stock could be seen as a "bet on the future of mankind." He's "obviously overegging it," Wilson continued, before noting that "even a tiny fraction of that amount makes SpaceX incredibly valuable." However, Wilson added that SpaceX is "massively exposed to AI bubble risk and relies on the debt financing bandwagon to keep rolling." He recommended investors treat the X post as a "bit of classic Musk hype and theatre," and instead "focus on what's going on under the hood." No comments right now, check back later. The unsolicited offer pushed Onsemi to switch its Synaptics deal to $123 a share in cash. Chipmaker Cirrus Logic made a surprise offer for Synaptics last month, trying to break up its agreed sale to Onsemi, Liana Baker and Yiqin Shen reported for Bloomberg. Cirrus Logic is the ‘Party A’ named in an updated Synaptics filing on Thursday, people familiar with the matter told Bloomberg. It is unclear whether Cirrus is still interested. Onsemi agreed to buy Synaptics in June in an all-stock deal then valued at about $7bn. Cirrus Logic’s bid used cash and shares. In response, Onsemi changed its offer last week to $123 a share, all in cash, which values the deal at about $5.7bn. Onsemi said at the time that it had acted after an “unsolicited competing proposal”, without naming the bidder. The filing shows Synaptics’ board took the Cirrus bid seriously and held talks. It decided Onsemi’s revised offer was better for shareholders. Synaptics makes chips for touch, display and connected devices. Onsemi wants the deal to push into chips for smart devices. Cirrus Logic, best known for audio chips in iPhones, has a market value of about $5.4bn, a little more than Synaptics’ $4.8bn. Its shares fell about 6% on Friday. Cirrus Logic and Onsemi declined to comment to Bloomberg. The Onsemi deal is expected to close by mid-2027. Anna Soellner, who ran corporate communications at Nvidia, has left after about four months, Geoff Weiss reported for Business Insider. Soellner joined the chipmaker around June, according to her LinkedIn profile. Her boss was Mylene Mangalindan, who leads the team, Axios reported in July. It is not clear why she left. She joined as Nvidia grew fast and faced close public scrutiny. In that time, the company agreed to buy Hugging Face for nearly $13bn. It also reported quarterly revenue of $96bn, Business Insider noted. When she joined, Soellner said she was honoured to help tell the story of “one of the world’s most consequential companies”. Before Nvidia, Soellner spent more than eight years running communications at Reddit. She helped steer it through its 2024 stock market debut. She also worked at the Motion Picture Association and the Center for American Progress. She was a senior adviser at the US Treasury. Nvidia did not respond to Business Insider’s request for comment. Tech > Mobile Starlink Mobile satellites could eventually improve enough to pass their signals through walls, dense foliage, and hilly terrain.  				Edited by Gael Cooper  October 10, 2026, 1:56 pm ET Elon Musk’s reach spans multiple global industries, placing the billionaire (sometimes trillionaire, depending on the stock market) at the center of the electric-vehicle industry, space exploration, artificial intelligence and national politics. He’s already involved in telecommunications through his company SpaceX and its global satellite internet service, Starlink, but recent developments may soon expand his influence with satellite-to-cellular coverage. SpaceX announced on X Thursday that it has agreed to acquire nationwide 800 MHz low-band spectrum to help build Starlink Mobile into a major US cellular carrier. By acquiring these low-band airwaves, SpaceX said it aims to improve signal propagation, allowing satellite coverage to bypass physical obstacles like building walls, dense foliage, and hilly terrain “This is the last critical piece of the spectrum puzzle needed for SpaceX to provide complete phone coverage in America,” Musk posted on X. More from CNET A SpaceX representative did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Under the terms of Thursday’s announcement, SpaceX will acquire investment firm Grain Management’s nationwide 800 MHz low-band spectrum portfolio for an estimated $8 billion. The deal gives the satellite operator up to 14 megahertz of paired airwaves, enabling two-way data transmission between satellites and mobile devices. The acquisition remains subject to approval by the Federal Communications Commission, which has not yet set a timeline for a decision. Acquiring the low-band spectrum is crucial for Starlink Mobile’s cellular ambitions. Unlike the high-frequency beams used currently, these low-band airwaves possess the physical properties required to pierce concrete walls, dense foliage and urban infrastructure, effectively solving the indoor dead zone problem that has long limited satellite-to-phone connectivity. Also this week, the FCC gave SpaceX the go-ahead to launch 15,000 satellites, which the company said can deliver more than 100 times the bandwidth of its current satellites. These satellites are direct to device, meaning that they can transmit phone calls, texts and other data straight from space to devices on the ground. SpaceX said the new satellites will bring “high-speed service directly to unmodified devices anywhere in the world.” For people looking for an alternative to the big three cellphone carriers AT&T, T-Mobile and Verizon Wireless, Starlink Mobile could eventually be an option. If and when the FCC approves the deal with Grain Management, Starlink Mobile will combine its newly acquired low-band spectrum with a massive, freshly approved fleet of 15,000 next-generation satellites. This hybrid network will use a mix of satellite beams and ground infrastructure to penetrate walls and eliminate indoor dead zones across the US while leveraging its high-bandwidth frequencies to deliver high-speed data directly to ordinary mobile devices. SpaceX plans to accelerate deployment of the new system next year. But according to analyst Tim Farrar, an industry expert with research firm Telecom, Media and Finance Associates, simply acquiring low-spectrum bandwidth in this week’s deal won’t be enough to compete strongly against AT&T, T-Mobile and Verizon Wireless, which uses thousands of cellphone towers. “It’s still a very limited amount of spectrum, and to get reliable building penetration in urban areas, SpaceX would have to deploy towers on the ground,” Farrar told CNBC. Last month, T-Mobile’s chief financial officer, Peter Osvaldik, dismissed the idea that Starlink’s satellite-to-cell service could adequately compete with the traditional wireless coverage offered by the major carriers. “It’s not a competitive threat,” Osvaldik said at the Global TMT Conference. “By the time the signal has gotten to your phone, you have no signal strength left,” he added. “You can have a million satellites up there with all the spectrum in the world, you can’t break the fundamental laws of physics.”   		© 2026 CNET, a Ziff Davis company. Gen Xers are putting their credit cards to work. The Federal Reserve's latest accounting of consumer finances finds that as of 2025, 45 to 54-year-olds had the largest credit card balances among age groups, surpassing 64 to 75-year-olds. At the same time, their younger millennial peers have been paying down debt, with balances for 35 to 44-year-olds falling. The latest data comes as the country's forgotten middle-child generation contends with its own mixed financial fortunes. Consumer sentiment is lowest among Americans ages 35 to 54, according to the University of Michigan's index, with sentiment among that millennial-Gen X cohort sliding below both their younger and older counterparts in the same period that their credit card balances began to tick up. For 45- to 54-year-olds, inflation-adjusted balances rose from around $3,300 in 2022 to around $5,100 in 2025, bringing them above their older peers, who previously had the highest debt. Even so, the 45- to 54-year-old cohort remains the highest paid in the economy. Per the Survey of Consumer Finances, their median pre-tax income is nearly $109,000, the highest among all age groups; it's also the largest median income ever recorded in the dataset after adjusting for inflation, meaning that Gen Xers are reaching new earnings heights. One source of stress for the Gen X cohort could be lagging overall wealth, despite their high incomes. Their older peers' median assets, which include things like stocks, bonds, and retirement accounts, have risen since 2022, bolstering their net worths. In particular, the median value of directly held stocks by the oldest Americans has soared by nearly $15,000 since 2022, while the value of stocks for 45 to 54-year-olds remains below 2019 levels. That means that the wealthiest Americans aren't those earning the highest incomes. Instead, it's the retirement-aged group holding onto increasingly valuable stocks and retirement accounts. The median net worth of those 75 and older rose from around $366,000 to nearly $505,000, while the 45-54 group saw its median edge down from around $270,000 to $255,000. And so, the generational wealth gap might be playing out not through the checks that workers are bringing home, but in the stock market and in the moments when Gen Xers find themselves swiping plastic in the face of rising costs. This week, Amazon unveiled a new lineup of Alexa Tablets. They no longer run a proprietary OS with a custom App Store, and instead embrace Android with a stock feel – while offering the Play Store. It’s a big shift in direction for Amazon. The tablets also look quite beautiful, while previous Fire tablets have felt cheap. I think these have the opportunity to do quite well. First and foremost, I want to make it quite clear that I’m not saying the iPad is doomed or anything remotely close to that. However, I do think the Alexa Tablet serves as a real form of iPad competition, which the iPad has generally lacked. Amazon is putting a lot of care into these tablets that other Android manufacturers haven’t, and while these tablets come in at lower price points – they certainly punch above their weight class. There are three Alexa Tablets to start off the lineup: an 8.7” model at $229, an 11” model at $329, and a 12” Pro model at $499. To me, the one in the middle is the most interesting. It offers 8GB of RAM, a 90Hz display, a thin design, and a similarly sharp display. That compares to the budget iPad, which comes in $120 higher with less RAM, a lesser display, and a thicker design. Granted, the iPad has the A16 chip, which probably feels much faster than the MediaTek chip powering it. The iPad also starts at 128GB, compared to the 64GB on the Alexa Tablet. Once you upgrade the Alexa Tablet to 128GB, there’s only a $70 difference. Hardware wise, the Alexa Tablets seem pretty competent. Obviously, Android on tablets isn’t going to be quite perfect, but given its tie in with Alexa and the fact that the tablet is priced quite well, I could see a lot of people wanting to buy these, even if they potentially would’ve considered iPads. Of course, one strong suit from Amazon is the Kindle experience, and these Alexa Tablets offer a reader mode that cuts blue light. Only time will tell, but Amazon might make a pretty big dent into the tablet market with its new entries. Even the 12” Pro at $499 seems like a really worthwhile product. At the very least, I hope some strong competition means Apple will be less complacent with its iPad upgrades. For example, the iPad Air has largely only received chip upgrades since its last redesign in 2020. If it’s a tablet running Android, it’s not competition for the iPad. The developer support still just isn’t there. I’m personally excited to try one of these out and truly put it to the test. Right now, Amazon also offers 20% off with any trade-in, making it an even better deal. What do you think of these new Alexa Tablets? Would you consider getting one of these for a friend or family member during the holiday season? Sound off in the comments. Over 20 years of combined experience and the latest in technology, AI,… Kalshi, Polymarket and the Coalition for Prediction Markets spent at least $3 million on lobbying and political contributions in 2026, as the companies and state officials fight over who can regulate prediction markets. The platforms say their contracts fall under federal oversight, while states argue they are gambling products governed by state law. The CFTC has sued states seeking to enforce gambling laws against prediction-market platforms, adding a federal dimension to the dispute. State officials have also organized to preserve their authority, including through a push for state control of prediction markets. OpenSecrets’ review of filings found that Kalshi gave $147,500 to the Republican Attorneys General Association and $170,000 to the Democratic Attorneys General Association in the first half of 2026. It also contributed $100,000 to the Republican Governors Association and $150,000 to the Democratic Governors Association during that period. Kalshi had at least one registered lobbyist in 41 states as of September, with nearly all hired since April. Its disclosed California lobbying spending reached $62,000 in the first half of the year; in New York, payments to two outside lobbying groups and in-house lobbyist Blake Bee were projected to top $400,000 through July 2027. The company also spent nearly $1 million on federal lobbying through June 30. That included $240,000 paid to Miller Strategies and $120,000 to Lincoln Policy Group, while Polymarket spent $180,000 on federal lobbying in 2026. Kalshi co-founders Tarek Mansour and Luana Lopes Lara collectively contributed about $1 million to Democratic and Republican recipients during the election cycle, according to federal filings cited by OpenSecrets. Kalshi has disclosed lobbying on the Prediction Market Act, the Protect College Sports Act and the National Defense Authorization Act. The disclosure does not specify the company’s position on those bills; the NDAA provisions described in OpenSecrets’ reporting would address certain prediction-market transactions, trading by Defense Department personnel and bets on military operations. The legal conflict has grown alongside prediction markets’ rapid expansion over the past two years. The platforms characterize their event contracts as swaps regulated by the CFTC, while states argue they operate like sportsbooks or casinos, which fall under state gambling laws. In July, 44 state attorneys general signed a letter to the CFTC opposing federal preemption of state gambling rules and describing prediction markets as a new kind of casino. Several lawsuits over the reach of state law have reached federal courts, and judges have split, leaving the question unresolved in the available reporting. Kalshi’s bipartisan contributions have drawn attention because state attorneys general are among the officials challenging the industry’s regulatory position. A company spokesperson told OpenSecrets that Kalshi supports candidates from both parties. Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield and Vermont Attorney General Charity Clark told local outlets that political donations had not influenced them. The wider federal scrutiny of prediction markets also includes an industry coalition. Kalshi joined Robinhood, Coinbase, Crypto.com and Underdog to launch the Coalition for Prediction Markets in December 2025; Polymarket is not a member. The coalition had paid $100,000 to federal lobbyists and spent $50,000 lobbying in California through June 30, according to the reporting. Kalshi’s state lobbying is concentrated in part on California and New York, where its disclosures cover legislation and work involving executive offices. OpenSecrets’ analysis said the broader state presence could help the company respond if courts ultimately allow states to regulate prediction markets as gambling; Polymarket had not registered state lobbyists at the time of the report. The dispute is moving through federal courts, but the reporting does not identify a filed Supreme Court petition or scheduled hearing. For now, the core question remains whether federal regulation displaces state gambling laws, while the companies continue lobbying at both levels and state officials press their case in court and in policy discussions. As mortgage rates continue to reach new heights, options for first-time buyers are dwindling. Even starter homes — affordable properties that entice first-time homebuyers get their foot in the door — are jumping in price.  The inventory of starter homes has recently decreased across the country. Data from Realtor.com shows that the national starter home share dropped from 38.1% to 36.2% from August 2019 to 2026, but the price during that timeframe increased 30.8%, from about $260,000 to $340,000. Realtor defines starter homes as homes listed at or below 80% of the median list price in that metro. A recent report from Realtor analyzing 8,300 ZIP codes in the largest 100 metros found that only 18.3% of those ZIP codes were starter-home dominant. "Affordability is only part of the story. What matters as much is whether affordable homes are actually for sale in the places where buyers want and need to live," Realtor senior economist Hannah Jones said. "For first-time buyers, the search is increasingly shaped by the geography of opportunity, not simply a metro's headline price. Keeping homeownership within reach will require more entry-level homes at attainable price points." It could be a while before the housing market gets back to "normal," but there are still areas that have more starter homes than others. When Trump Accounts became available, Gene Goldman was on board. The chief investment officer of Cetera Investment Management opened accounts for his twin girls, born earlier this year, giving each access to the $1,000 government contribution and a diversified stake in the market. But now, the accounts he signed up for could look a little different. The Treasury Department is now allowing companies and other donors to gift individual stocks to children's Trump Accounts. What's raised some eyebrows is that shares can't be declined or sold for five years. Goldman said that changes the "character of the program" from a "simple, diversified vehicle" to one that could leave children with "single-stock exposure." There is still a lot of upside with a gifted stock, Goldman said. "A child gets part ownership in a business at no cost, and it can grow tax-deferred for decades," he said, potentially "adding up to a lot by adulthood." But many prickly issues and concerns could come up for parents, from taxes and investment risk to workplace compliance. And, maybe most importantly, what can you do if you don't want the stock? After all, as part of the rollout of this new stock donation rule, the Treasury Department also opened new accounts for more than 60 million American children, without their parents needing to sign up. (Those born from 2025 to 2028 are eligible for the $1,000 government contribution, but their parents will still need to claim it.) The Treasury declined to comment for this story."This is the most generational thing we've done for youth," IRS CEO and Social Security administrator Frank Bisignano said on CNBC Thursday, noting that donations already lined up range from "small to mega." Stock donations could make some children serious cash a couple of decades from now, but they are not free of considerations. Here's what four financial planning experts said parents should know. Soon enough, there will be parents who find out that not only is their child a Trump Account holder, but their child owns some stock. So how did the stock get there? It's not as if donors like Gwynne Shotwell, SpaceX's president, who pledged to donate $300 million in SpaceX stock, can just decide to place money in the accounts of specific children straight from their own personal accounts. Donations can only come from a tax-exempt nonprofit, known as a 501(c)(3), a private foundation, or a donor-advised fund. It can target a group as small as 5,000 children based on characteristics such as ZIP code, family income, and age. The Treasury Department also needs to approve the donations, and, unsurprisingly, the donated stocks must be of American companies. It's not novel for individual donors to donate stocks to a charity, said Brian Boswell, senior wealth advisor from Savvy Advisors. It's long been a way to give highly taxed shares to charity, deduct the full-market value as a charitable gift, and "never pay capital gains tax on the growth." Given the size of the donations, donors are likely to be quite wealthy and potentially rare. Boswell said he doesn't expect to see the donations too often. "It suits a small group of high-net-worth donors with large, low-basis public stock positions (founders and early employees after an IPO, for example) who already give through a foundation or donor-advised fund," he told Business Insider. Once the stock is in the Trump account, it operates similarly to a traditional IRA. It continues to appreciate in value, and there are no tax considerations until money is withdrawn from the account. There's no way to decline the individual stock, and no way to sell until it's been held for 5 years or the child holding the account turns 18. For account holders whose parents work in industries like financial services, government, or journalism, which can have strict rules about stock ownership, this creates a new compliance headache. Tim Steffen, director of advanced planning at Baird Private Wealth Management, has to follow strict rules with his own investments. With a few exceptions, like a spouse's employer-based retirement plan or certain 529 college savings plans, his accounts have to be managed by his firm. "An account that we're investing in and managing that's held away from our firm is not something that's looked kindly on in general," Steffen told Business Insider. Such rules prevent financial advisors from using the confidential information they learn in the course of their job to make money. Don't fret if you have to follow these rules; Steffen expects employers with strict compliance regimes to make Trump accounts another exception. "Each employer and each industry is going to have to figure out how to address the individual stock issue," Steffen said, especially as you have almost no control over these allocations. As the rules are now, even if your child receives stock in a company you have an ideological or financial reason to oppose, you're stuck with it. The rules raise theoretical possibilities for influence or unwanted ownership. A company closing a factory could give stock to children in the surrounding community. A business trying to win support for a major local project could make nearby children shareholders. Or, more simply, a donor could give children shares in a company their parents might actively avoid, like a defense contractor or tobacco company. The biggest financial risk here, Goldman said, is "putting too many eggs in one basket." "The best approach is to treat it as a bonus on top of a diversified core, not a replacement for one," he said. Christina Taylor, vice president of tax development and delivery at fintech company April, said that at the end of the holding period, the shares could be sold and the money can be put into a diversified vehicle, while "any gains from the holding period stay in the account to continue growing." "The child gets money they didn't have before, with no tax due when it goes in and years of tax-deferred growth ahead," she said. As for tax implications, it's very similar to an employer making a matching contribution to your 401(k), said Steffen. That means any money not put in by the family will be treated as income and will be fully taxable when withdrawn. "If the only thing you ever have in the account is the $1,000 that you got from the federal government, or maybe one of these charitable gifts, then yes, every penny that comes out would be totally taxed," Steffen said. Just like IRAs, capital gains growth will likely be taxed as ordinary income when the money is withdrawn, said Taylor, with the same 10% penalty for early withdrawals before you're close to retirement age. The reality, though, says Taylor, is that all of this is subject to change, with Treasury still taking comments on the rule changes, which are also temporary and will expire in 2029. She expects more tweaks before it's finalized, after all, we're already far afield of the original pitch. "Congress set these accounts up to hold diversified, low-cost index funds, so letting a donor pick an individual stock is a big departure from their original intent," Taylor said. Most of your digital life revolves around your daily drivers — your phone, computer, and maybe even a tablet. They're the devices you probably spent a lot of time carefully choosing to make sure they're a perfect fit for your lifestyle and needs. More often than not, though, you overlook an important part of your setup: accessories that keep your daily drivers powered and convenient to use. Jean-Christophe Laloux said Europe’s Tech Champions Initiative is set to back smaller funds too, likely from November. AI, biotech, defence and cleantech are the EIF’s focus. Jean-Christophe Laloux of the European Investment Bank at Wave by Vento in Turin, 9 October 2026 Europe must give its startups the capital to grow without leaving the continent, Jean-Christophe Laloux said. The incoming chief executive of the European Investment Fund spoke at Wave by Vento in Turin on Friday. “It’s not enough to innovate in Europe. You also must be able to scale in Europe. And that is really important on the notion of sovereignty,” Laloux said. Sovereignty does not mean protectionism or isolationism, he said. It means offering European alternatives where things really matter, from critical raw materials to cyber resilience. Laloux is director general for EU lending and advisory operations at the European Investment Bank. He takes over the EIF, the bank group’s venture arm, on 1 January, the EIF said in July. Ian King of The Times interviewed him. The bottleneck has moved from early-stage innovation to scaling up, Laloux said. That is the growth stage, from Series B to C. The European Tech Champions Initiative was set up to close that gap, he said. It is a fund of funds of nearly €4bn, backed by six member states and the EIB Group. It invests in venture funds of about €1bn. Funds that size can write bigger cheques, so companies that have raised Series A and B can grow faster and stay in Europe. At the same event, Vittorio Colao told reporters that Europe needs a single capital market. The initiative has backed 12 funds, he said, nearly three times the number of €1bn funds in Europe five years ago. Those funds already hold 15 European unicorns. Laloux expects to announce a second version in November. It will also back funds of €300m to €500m, because not every ecosystem has funds that reach €1bn. It will add a platform for institutional and private investors to co-invest alongside the funds. Italy put €150m into the initiative. The funds it backs have invested nearly €600m in seven Italian companies, three of them with international partners, Laloux said. That shows international investors find the Italian ecosystem interesting, he said. The EIB Group also lends to startups through venture debt, he said. It has no repayment for at least five years, and instead of high interest, the lender takes warrants or similar rewards tied to the company’s success. The group also structures the equity side of the European Innovation Council’s funding for early-stage startups. Deep tech in Europe has grown from about €1tn in valuation five years ago to €4tn, faster than any other part of the economy, Laloux said. He named climate, security and defence, space and biotech. Funds that received EIB Group money backed Isar Aerospace, he said, whose Spectrum rocket launched from Norway. Security and defence, including cybersecurity, is where capital and valuations have grown most in the past year, he said. The EIF will focus on four areas where Europe still leads: AI, health and biotech, security and defence, and cleantech. On AI, Europe cannot afford to be left out, because it can lift productivity, he said. Europe must neither leave AI unregulated nor smother it with rules. The EIB has earmarked €3bn for the EU’s AI gigafactories, he said.                                        Cristian Dina is the CRO at The Next Web. How frontier labs, neolabs, and investors can all win Neolabs today are being asked to pull off two moonshots at once. Their investors want both a research breakthrough and a venture-scale business, even though each of those alone is a 1 in 100 outcome. Asking for both makes their chances 1 in 10,000. I think there’s a better alternative, one that borrows from the way pharma handles risky R&D and lets frontier labs, neolabs, and investors all come out ahead. Today, OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google DeepMind are caught in a neck-and-neck race on model quality and intelligence. Every release needs to exceed expectations, or at least meet what competitors are doing. So they’d rather spend their resources scaling things that are proven to work, like improving data pipelines, building infrastructure for larger runs, and buying ever-more compute. However, researchers often want to work on “the next big thing”, new paradigms that could lead to a discontinuous jump in intelligence. As a result, there’s often tension between what the market needs them to ship and what researchers want to focus on. In the past year, many senior researchers who want to pursue these bets have started neolabs, nascent AI startups focused on big research bets, usually funded with a lot of money before they have a product or revenue, so they can pay for compute and salaries. That way they can chase the big idea with venture-scale resources. On the surface, investors are betting that a neolab becomes the next OpenAI or Anthropic. They remind themselves that Anthropic was once a neolab too, started by a group of researchers who left OpenAI and raised hundreds of millions of dollars before they had a product. Privately though, most of them will admit the odds of a repeat are next to none, even with world-class researchers and engineers. Running a research team is a different job from scaling a company. Researchers usually aren’t great at product, go-to-market, operations, logistics, etc., all the things that traditionally matter for a sustainable company. (Ali Ghodsi at Databricks is a good exception.) However, neolabs are expected to do both: make a breakthrough and scale a product. Sometimes this splits a company in two, with half the people wanting to build and sell and the other half wanting to do research and build ASI. Focus and alignment are the biggest advantages a startup has over better-funded incumbents, but this expectation can take a toll on both. Investors who expect their neolab to do both will likely be disappointed when it does neither. One radical move is to admit that a neolab is just going to do world-class, groundbreaking research. Expect close to zero revenue and let them cook. If they succeed, they get acquired or acquihired. The catch is that this doesn’t work for investors. A VC needs companies that can return the entire fund, and it’s hard to promise LPs that an acquihire will do that, especially at the sky-high multibillion valuations neolabs raise at today. Drug development has dealt with a similar problem for decades. Companies regularly risk hundreds of millions of dollars in R&D on a drug that might pay off billions. A drug can pass early trials and still fail before FDA approval, usually because it doesn’t work well enough, and sometimes because of side effects or manufacturing problems. Pharma handles this by splitting the work. Smaller biotech companies take on the risk of discovery and development. If a drug works, a big pharma company acquires the startup or buys the drug as IP. The big company doubles down on what it’s good at, which is producing and distributing drugs at scale. The small company gets to do the science without having to invent a business model. A small biotech’s business model comes down to one question: can we make this drug work or not? The division of labor works. Of the drugs the FDA approved from 2013 to 2022, small companies with under \$500M in revenue originated 52%, while the biggest companies, with over \$10B in revenue, originated 36%1. Biotech investors have made money this way for decades. Many of their biggest wins come from getting acquired, not from growing into the next Pfizer. What’s missing today is a promise. The people who start, join, or fund a neolab need to know, before they take the risk, that a big payoff is waiting if the research works. Frontier labs could make that promise ahead of time through pre-registered acquisitions. This kind of promise is also called “pull funding”. Push funding pays for research up front, like a grant or a VC round. Pull funding promises to pay for the result once it exists. In 1714, the British government promised £20,000 to anyone who could find a ship’s longitude at sea, and a self-taught clockmaker named John Harrison responded by inventing a clock that kept accurate time on a rolling ship. In 2009, five countries and the Gates Foundation promised \$1.5B to any company that could supply poor countries with pneumococcal vaccines at \$3.50 a dose or less, and vaccine makers responded with enough supply to immunize more than 150 million children. Big companies have always bought startups for their patents or their people. What’s different about AI research is the cost of finding out whether an idea works. A software founder can test an idea on a laptop. Testing a new training method at a scale that matters takes a training run that can cost tens or hundreds of millions of dollars, and the cost of the largest runs has grown 2.4x a year since 2016. Nobody spends that much on a guess without knowing what success is worth. The stakes are also bigger than any one company’s exit. A breakthrough in how models learn ends up in systems that hundreds of millions of people use every day, so how we pay for that research decides how fast it happens and who gets to do it. I can see this playing out in two ways: In both cases, the target can be a new capability, like a benchmark score, or something the lab can’t easily build itself, like a dataset, a set of RL environments, or a regulatory approval. Here’s what an open offer could look like. Say a frontier lab posts: “We’ll acquire any team that matches our last-generation model on this eval suite using a tenth of the training compute, for \$2B. Train from scratch, no distilling from anyone’s frontier model, and the offer is good through 2027.” The price makes sense, because the largest training runs are on track to cost more than \$1B each by 2027, so cutting the compute for every future run by 10x is worth far more than \$2B. The obvious question is why a lab would name a price before seeing results, when it could wait and buy whatever works. After a breakthrough, it’s too late. Training recipes can’t be patented, so once a team shows a lab how it did something, the lab doesn’t need the team anymore. No sensible team will show its work without a price agreed first, and no lab will pay for something it hasn’t seen. This is called Arrow’s information paradox. Naming the price in advance breaks the deadlock: the team knows what it gets, and the lab gets to check the result before it pays. Pre-registered acquisitions let everyone come out ahead. The frontier labs get to: Neolabs and their researchers get to: Investors get to: An open offer is also a floor, not a ceiling. If a team hits the target and would rather build a business around what it made, it can turn the offer down. Some version of this already exists. Every past acquisition and acquihire, like Google’s \$2.4B Windsurf deal, sets an implicit anchor for what a research team can exit for, and neolabs point to those anchors to justify their valuations. A pre-registered acquisition just makes that explicit, reducing the uncertainty for everyone. Right now a neolab has to win at research and at business, two moonshots at once. Put a price on the breakthrough and it only has to win one. The payoff is smaller than becoming the next Anthropic, but the odds go from 1 in 10,000 to 1 in 100, and that’s a bet you can build a team around. So, frontier labs: what would you pay for a training run that costs a tenth as much? Name a price. One caveat: A drug is easy to patent, and an AI training recipe mostly isn’t. So in AI the payoff can’t just be a sale of IP. It has to be an acquisition, either of the team itself or of a moat that’s hard to copy, like regulatory approvals, unique data, or unique physical infrastructure. ↩︎

It was my lifelong dream to live in New York City. Wild, given that I was born in a small rural town in Australia, where I grew up riding dirt bikes, not reading fashion magazines. The Land Down Under was a big, beautiful place offering an idyllic, laid-back beach life, but I always felt a pull toward The Big Apple. That lust further ignited in the '90s as I watched the city depicted in shows like "Friends" and "Sex and the City." So in 2014, on the cusp of turning 40, I dragged my husband, our Bengal cat, and our two sons — then 2 and 9 — to New York. We told ourselves we'd come for a year, for an adventure. Twelve years later, I'm still here. It's certainly been one hell of a (ridiculously expensive) ride. In New York City, rental costs are no joke. We traded our beautiful 1890s cottage — three-bedroom, two-bath, front porch, huge yard, tree-lined street, 10 minutes from Bondi Beach — for a two-bedroom loft apartment in Tribeca that cost us $8,000 a month. (This is not unusual for a two-bed in this neighborhood.) By comparison, the monthly mortgage on our cottage in Sydney was, after conversion, less than half of that price. Still, we knew we were choosing to live in a more expensive neighborhood in Lower Manhattan, and we did so because it felt like a great place to raise our kids. We loved the community, the quiet cobblestone streets, and the access to Hudson River Park. Our loft was essentially a large box, with windows only at the front. It was also a fifth-floor walk-up, and between the angry downstairs neighbors who complained constantly about the sound of kids moving around and the fact that I had to carry a toddler and a stroller up five brutal flights of stairs, we left in under a year. We moved around the corner to another loft, this one even more expensive, and lasted a little over a year until the building was condemned and we had to move — again. At one point, my husband and I had considered buying a property in NYC with our nest egg, but we didn't have a clue how to navigate the competitive real-estate market, and it seemed clear we'd only get a teeny apartment for our budget. The math didn't add up, and the risk of owning freaked us out. So we kept rolling the dice on renting. Between my husband and me separating, the kids outgrowing smaller apartments, and landlords unexpectedly hiking up the rent, I've moved about 10 times since coming to the US. A financial reprieve in NYC is that public education is free, though school admissions can be complicated, with factors like zoning and lottery systems shaping where kids end up. Thankfully, both of my boys got into a highly regarded public school in Manhattan, and I was impressed with their education.  I was also glad we (mostly) dodged expensive private schools — except when my youngest attended a language-immersion school for about $30,000 a year. He came out knowing basic Mandarin, which would have been worth the investment — only he's since forgotten all of it. Then comes the killer: college. After graduating from high school, my oldest was accepted into a prestigious university in the Midwest to study engineering. Sure, he could've attended a more affordable or in-state school, but a lot of "New York rats" (that's what my boys proudly call themselves) want to leave the city they grew up in — and their parents — to go to college somewhere else. Getting into a respected college also felt like a major flex, and we all felt the pressure for him to attend, no matter the cost. So, his dad and I haggled over merit and financial aid and took out student loans to cover his first year. Add kitting out his dorm room, him blowing up our Seamless account (despite having a paid meal plan), and the costs of us flying out to visit and flying him home … year one probably cost around $70,000. He didn't end up staying after his first year, which meant our student loans were due far sooner than we planned. The silver lining of not completing his degree is that, unlike many college graduates in the US, he's not saddled with four years' worth of debt. Our rent, as established, doesn't leave much in the budget for vacations — or for airfare back to Australia to see family and friends. As Aussies, our ideal time to go home is around Christmas, when it's summer there, and many people are off work and school. However, that privilege can set us back upward of $4,000 in round-trip airfare alone for the four of us. On top of that, each way, we'd have to take two flights, totaling over 22 hours in the air. In my opinion, we need three weeks for a proper trip Down Under, especially as I have to visit my loved ones in two cities.  Considering our sons' public schools only granted about a week off around that time of year, it rarely seemed worth the money or jet lag. This also explains why we typically only make it home every other year. Some costs are even harder to reconcile with when living on a separate continent and in a different time zone from so many loved ones. From afar, I'm watching my mum age from 10,000 miles away (she just turned 80), and how my sister must carry the load of caring for our father as he faces health issues. There are so many milestone birthdays, weddings, funerals, and family events I've missed and can never get back. To be clear, a lot of these costs were tied to choices we made as we sought to give our family a certain kind of life in NYC. Despite the emotional and financial pain, do I regret moving? Not for a New York minute. This city has an incredible, lively vibe. We've forged deep friendships, created new traditions, and lapped up the electrifying culture on tap.  I also feel connected to the world in a way I never did in Australia; I can be in the Caribbean in about four hours, Europe in seven — and I've met people from all walks of life. There's an energy and diversity here you won't find anywhere else in the world, along with a feeling that you can do anything. Regardless of any financial regrets and mistakes from the past 12 years, New York City is home. No comments right now, check back later. Comments are unavailable right now. Jump to

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Samuel Sévigny, 32, the cofounder and marketing director at Chaletô, a short-term rental property management company based in Quebec, Canada. Sévigny started Chaletô in 2022 with four of his friends and has scaled to over 500 cabins and condos. The following has been edited for length and clarity. It started as six friends fresh out of college. We all had other jobs. It was in 2016, and we wanted to invest in real estate, diversify, and get started in life. One of our co-founders had condos in downtown Quebec City already, so he pitched us the idea of investing all together and building our own cabin, and to manage it ourselves. So that's what we did. We launched our first cabin together in 2019, then our second in 2020, right in the middle of COVID. Fast-forward to 2022, and we had four different units that we owned and managed, and we wanted to delegate the process of managing them. We couldn't find anyone who was professional enough for our standards, so it was just like most origin stories: it starts with a problem that we're trying to solve. In the meantime, our neighbor started pressuring us, asking if we could manage his property because he could see that we were rented pretty much the whole year. We said no at first, but he kept asking. At some point, we decided to say yes. It started with our neighbor, then it was the neighbor's neighbor, and then the whole street. Then we had 10 properties under management in 2022. The six of us had to sit down and say, "Hey, what are we going to do with this? It's getting serious." Either we'll make this a serious, legitimate business, or we stop, because there's no in-between. So in 2022, we decided to incorporate Chaletô. We grew from 10 to 500-plus units in four years. We decided to make it a real thing and to go all-in. Take a smarter break in your day - and see how far you get. The biggest difference between an individual host and a property management company is really the optimization at scale. When you're a professional host, you're dealing with your own cleaner, your tech stack is under one roof, and you've got one or two listings. You're paying the higher-bracket price for all the tools you're using. You probably decide to cut different tools because you maybe don't have the resources, or the time, or the training to be able to use them well. I'm thinking about dynamic pricing tools. I'm thinking about AI automation for operations. I'm thinking about a bunch of things like that, because that's not your day job. I was working in advertising in Montreal and doing Airbnb hosting on the side. I was managing the guest messaging on nights and weekends, so I really lived the individual host dilemma of having a full-time job and then dealing with guests Friday and Saturday when you're off from your day job. I lived through that for several years, so I really, really understand how it feels. When you make this a full-time gig and it becomes a full-time business, then you make gains at scale. You get a little bit more leverage with relationships within the industry. For example, you can negotiate cleaners' contracts a little bit easier. That comes with professional management, and that's the main benefit of having it at scale. Also, you can attract talent for specific things in your business that you couldn't if you were alone. If you're managing only one or two properties, there's no need to have a full-time dedicated revenue management person, someone who's trained for this, sophisticated, and educated about that. But when you manage 50 or 100 properties, it becomes interesting because you can optimize each function of your hosting business. When you scale, it's easy to get distracted. You see it in every industry possible: real estate, service, and tech. It's like when something starts clicking, and it works, and everything seems to be working for you, then the easiest shortcut for entrepreneurs, I think, is jumping on all the opportunities. It would be easy for us to say, "We're going to keep investing in real estate because we're giving the service to support it," but it's a different beast. Investing is totally different than servicing the owners. Now you're distracted between two different businesses: you're scaling one, and then you're trying to scale the other. Another problem we face is the speed at which AI is moving, not only for our industry but for everyone. At what stage does it become mature enough to be implemented within our business, and where do you focus? Because it seems like there is a new tool and there's a new shiny object being created by the next engineer every other week. One of our challenges is always, do you keep hiring people and training them and keep it very hospitality based, or do you optimize with AI, and is it mature enough to support that optimization, or is it just a super shiny object and a gamble? So far, I'll say I don't think we have 100% the right answer to that. We prefer to hire and grow our team for now and really double down on service when everyone's running towards AI. We also prefer to hire actual people from Quebec. They speak French first, English second, and they can support any type of customer service issue because they live here, they understand the market, they understand the region, and the experiences around it. We use tech to support our business, but every couple of months, it feels like you have to re-challenge yourself. Is this still the right tech? Are you overpaying for it? Conversable Economist Many of us are inconsistent in our economic desires. I would like the price of my home to rise, because it increases my wealth, but I would also like the prices of all other homes to fall, so that I could sell my house and buy an even nicer house. Also, I would like to have the value of my house rise, but also pay lower property taxes.  David Schleicher digs into the second issue in “The Great American Property Tax Freak Out” (posted online at SSRN on September 1, 2026). He writes:  In the last three years, a number of states have substantially reformed their property tax systems, providing huge tax benefits to owner-occupied homes and shifting the burden of paying for services like schools and police to commercial property owners (including rental apartment buildings), to other local taxes, and to state funding, which itself largely comes from sources like sales taxes and income taxes. A few, including Florida, Ohio, North Dakota, and Texas, have considered going further, either completely abandoning property taxation for owner-occupied housing or even abandoning property taxation entirely. … One might think that homeowners would be happy that their largest asset has appreciated substantially in value, as homes did, particularly in suburbs, in the post-COVID period. But because property taxes are wealth taxes, property owners have responded to their increasing wealth with political anger, pushing shifts in property tax policy, often leading to increasing rates on commercial property owners who have seen declining values during the same period. … [T]hese reforms shift the property tax from a tool homeowners use collectively to provide for locally-wanted services towards a more standard form of redistributive taxation, charging commercial property owners to pay for services for homeowners. Further, they will lead to greater state authority over local governments, less stable funding for local governments (but also less tax foreclosure in recessions), and stricter zoning controls (but more building of homes where it is legal). Perhaps most notably, these property tax reforms will lead to higher housing costs, and thus constitute a substantial transfer of  wealth towards people who already own homes and have already seen their net worth increase substantially in the post COVID housing market. A few other facts and insights seem worth appending here.  1) there’s a lot of local variation across public finance in the United States. But as a broad statement, property taxes are the major own-source of revenue for local US governments, and in turn the main source of financing for local schools. Many local governments have traditionally relied on property taxes to pay for police as well. The political dynamic of reducing property taxes often involves state-level actions that limit or block property taxes at the local level. It is not clear that voters for lower property taxes have drawn a connection in their mind to the likelihood of reduced local public services.  2) the property tax is a form of wealth tax, and it has the standard problems of a wealth tax: specifically, you can have more wealth–say, the value of your home, your business, or your retirement account went up–without having immediate income to pay a higher level of taxes. Thus, older voters who tend to have higher accumulated wealth, partly in the form of home equity, but also lower current income, are a politically powerful and sympathetic group in the push to reduce or eliminate property taxes.   3) If property taxes are reduced or abolished, the cost of owning a home falls. (For example, imagine that you could guarantee that the roof, exterior, driveway, plumbing and HVAC systems in your house would never need repair or replacement, which would also lead to a fall in the cost of owning a home.) With lower costs of owning a home, the market value of the home rises. Thus, the ironic outcome is that higher housing prices cause voters to want to limit or repeal property taxes, which would then lead to even higher housing prices. Moreover, the current homeowners who have already benefited from higher home values will benefit further, while homeownership will look even costlier for potential future homebuyers. Systematic Investment Plans (SIPs) are meant to help investors ride out market volatility, but the prolonged weakness in equities has pushed returns into the red. Here is how investors should approach their mutual fund SIPs, as reported by ET Bureau. SIPs spread investments across market levels but cannot shield investors from equity market falls. With the Nifty down around 13% from September-end 2024, corrections can push accumulated investments into negative returns if earlier instalments were made at higher valuations. While new SIPs buy more units at lower prices, the benefits may take time to reflect, especially in weak or range-bound markets. Long-term investors need not stop SIPs just because markets fall, as lower NAVs allow them to accumulate more units and potentially benefit from a recovery. However, increasing SIP contributions should depend on available savings, financial goals, asset allocation and the ability to withstand further market declines or prolonged weak returns.  Negative SIP returns over short periods are not necessarily a reason to stop investing, as market corrections can keep investments made at higher levels in the red. However, investors should distinguish between broader market weakness and fund-specific underperformance by reviewing their scheme’s returns against its benchmark and peers over comparable periods.  No. SIPs can be used across equity, hybrid and other mutual fund categories. While they are popular in equity funds for long-term investing, rupee-cost averaging is more noticeable in volatile markets, where regular investments buy varying numbers of units at different NAVs. OPPO's Find X10 Pro Max puts a 200MP camera behind each of its three main rear lenses, giving the ultrawide, main and telephoto cameras the same headline resolution. Its China-market configuration pairs that camera system with an 8,000mAh battery, a 6.78-inch display and MediaTek's Dimensity 9600 Pro processor. OPPO will launch the Find X10 series internationally on October 21 in Mallorca, Spain, with regional pricing and availability to follow at the event. All three Pro Max rear cameras support 4K at 120fps and 8K at 30fps. Open Gate recording gives creators extra room to crop the same footage for horizontal and vertical screens. Price: International pricing announced October 21Where to buy: OPPO (launch details; regional availability forthcoming) A 24mm-equivalent main camera leads the Hasselblad system with a 1/1.3-inch sensor and an f/1.5 lens. Beside it, the 13mm-equivalent ultrawide combines a 1/1.56-inch sensor, f/2.2 aperture and 124-degree field of view. That's the lens for fitting more of a landscape, building or group into the frame. For tighter framing, a 70mm-equivalent telephoto uses another 1/1.56-inch sensor with an f/2.1 lens. It provides 3x optical zoom and focuses as close as 10cm for macro photography. Both the main and telephoto cameras have optical image stabilization. Full-resolution 200MP shooting is available through Hasselblad's high-resolution mode at the three optical focal lengths. A separate second-generation Danxia color sensor adds 24 spectral sampling channels to the imaging system. OPPO also offers a separately sold Hasselblad teleconverter kit. That gives the phone an accessory route for longer-distance shooting, while the built-in telephoto remains a 3x optical camera. Rear video recording reaches 8K at 30 frames per second, including 10-bit Log recording for color grading. Dolby Vision capture goes up to 4K at 120fps. Open Gate recording is supported at the 0.5x, 1x and 3x optical focal lengths. It preserves more of the sensor's image area, leaving extra room to choose a landscape or portrait crop during editing. A single recording can supply both formats without committing to one orientation at capture. The front camera is a 50MP autofocus unit with an f/2.0 lens and support for 4K recording at up to 60fps. A separately sold OPPO Bubble preview screen provides another option for framing yourself with the rear cameras. The international announcement lists an 8,000mAh silicon-carbon battery, with a 7,150mAh battery in selected markets. OPPO has not identified those markets in the announcement. The China model has an 8,000mAh typical-capacity battery and supports up to 80W wired SuperVOOC charging, 50W wireless charging and 55W USB-C PPS charging. We may receive a commission on purchases made from links. Who knew that a ring of magnets built into a smartphone chassis would be so dang useful? We're referring, of course, to Apple's MagSafe technology, made its debut on the iPhone 12. Funny enough, Apple's first MagSafe foray was all the way back in 2006; the original MacBook Pro came with a magnetic charging cable that was designed to disconnect if someone tripped on the wire. Nowadays, MagSafe is a universal term for MacBooks and iPhone magnets, though an increasing number of Android phones and cases adopting similar magnetic accessory designs too. Whether you're rocking the latest iPhone generation or you're in the Android-only camp, there's a massive market of MagSafe accessories to choose from. The lion's share of these gadgets are mounts, wallets, and portable power banks, but we wanted to direct the spotlight toward a few lesser-known MagSafe attachments. It took some scouring on Amazon and interesting keyword research, but the clicks and scrolling paid off. We were able to track down five cool MagSafe gadgets that aren't mounts, wallets, or power banks. All five of our selections are sold on Amazon, and each item scored four stars or higher from customer reviews. From lighting when you need it most to a magnetized game controller, there's plenty to unpack, so let's dive in. Apple introduced its ProRes 422 HQ codec on the iPhone 13 Pro, and it's a glorious way to preserve as much image detail as possible when shooting videos. That bodes well for videographers and other workflows where you want minimal compression. One of the only drawbacks is how much storage a ProRes 422 HQ file eats up. The $40 Hagibis MC100 Pro SSD Enclosure aims to solve that problem. The device attaches via MagSafe and connects via USB-C to a compatible iPhone for power and data. The MC100 will interface with NVMe SSDs of up to 2TB that support the M-Key/M+B Key 2230 specification. The enclosure contains two 10Gbps USB-C ports, both of which are capable of 1,000-1,200Mbps for read and write speeds. That's fast enough to transfer an HD movie in as little as two seconds, according to the manufacturer. You can also use the USB-C ports to power other peripherals, such as a microphone or LED light. More than 260 Amazon shoppers wrote in about the Hagibis MC100, resulting in a 4.3-out-of-5-star rating. A couple of things to be aware of: the included USB-C cables aren't actually fast enough to record in 4K ProRes HQ, which can result in dropped frames. And depending on what type of SSD you purchase, you may need to use one of the enclosure's USB-C ports to power the disk. You never know when you're going to need an extra bit of illumination, so it might pay to keep the $16 ULANZI M10 Magnetic Selfie Light on standby. This MagSafe-ready light has five brightness levels and lighting modes, including a reading mode with reduced blue light. Once attached, the light can also be rotated up to 360 degrees, allowing flexibility to lock in the right angle. The ULANZI M10 contains a 400-milliamp rechargeable battery, which delivers up to 50 minutes at max brightness and up to 4.5 hours when the M10 is set to reading mode. The built-in USB-C port is how you'll recharge, and it only takes about 70 minutes to restore a fully depleted battery. You can also use the M10's reading mode while charging. Amazon shoppers gave the ULANZI M10 4.2 out of 5 stars, which is based on over 100 reviews. Several users thought it was a great addition to a non-backlit e-reader. One individual was glad that brightness and color temperature changes are saved when you turn the light off. There were a couple of reports of the M10 failing after just a few uses, but considering all the positive feedback, it's possible those are outliers. Snapping the perfect photo with a smartphone can be a challenge, especially since the flat-rectangle design isn't very ergonomic. Instead of dealing with cramped touchscreen controls and the occasional side button, you can invest in the $27 TELESIN Magnetic Phone Camera Grip. This MagSafe attachment makes portrait and landscape photography feel more natural, thanks in part to its camera-inspired finger hook design that provides comfort and stability. Conveniently, the TELESIN grip comes with a Bluetooth camera remote that maintains a connection with your phone up to 32 feet away. The grip is threaded, too, so you'll be able to mount it on a tripod for improved stationary photos or video. It also features a few buttons that handle orientation-switching, zoom, and shutter speed. The grip comes in matte white and black, and at the time of writing, you could apply a coupon for an extra $4 off either design. The Amazon crowd gave this TELESIN product 4.1 out of 5 stars, which is based on over 2,000 reviews. Many individuals praised the grip's ease of use and simple setup. One person did struggle with the zoom functionality on a Google Pixel 10 Pro XL. Another reviewer had similar issues with an iPhone 15 Pro Max, though they said the grip worked just fine with their Samsung Galaxy S24 Ultra. Modern game consoles are more expensive than they've ever been. To that end, many gamers are taking the retro route instead. Whether you're returning to a much-loved classic or emulating an older game you've never played before, the $50 abxylute M4 Snap-On Mobile Gaming Controller offers a compelling alternative to touchscreen controls. It's also easy to use: All you have to do is attach via MagSafe, fire it up, pair over Bluetooth, and start playing games. If you don't have MagSafe on your phone or case, the manufacturer includes a MagSafe sticker. The device is cross-compatible between iOS and Android, and you can choose from three control schemes: HID, PS, and NS. On a full charge, you can expect up to 12 hours of playtime. The abxylute M4 also works with a KeyLinker app to customize buttons and other device settings. Amazon shoppers gave the controller a 4-out-of-5-star rating, based on over 360 reviews. The overall consensus is that this is a great add-on for casual mobile gaming. One user had issues with Android button mapping, so it may have some hiccups. Wired headphones may not receive the same type of fanfare as their wireless counterparts, but you can't experience top-end audio codecs over Bluetooth; not without aptX Adaptive support, at any rate. If you're a fan of detail-rich formats like LDAC or Samsung Seamless Codec, and you do a lot of your music-listening via phone, $150 Fosi Audio MD3 Headphone Amplifier may offer a compelling option. In years past, external DACs like this one required an awkward dongle that would hang off your smartphone. Fortunately, Fosi Audio put MagSafe to good use for its hardware. Equipped with an ESS ES9039Q2M DAC and four amp chips, the MD3 supports up to 32-bit/384kHz PCM, as well as DSD256 playback. The MD3 also works well with many wired headphone options, though some reviews have mentioned that it's not quite powerful enough to drive an ultra-high-end set of planar cans. Another noteworthy feature is the MD3's pass-through charging thanks to its dual USB-C ports. Amazon user reviews were pretty happy with the Fosi Audio M3, too, giving it an aggregate 4.5-out-of-5-star score, based on more than 70 reviews. One individual praised the MD3's ability to drive multiple pairs of IEMs. Another user said they liked the quality of the leather backing used, which also helps to protect your phone case from scratches. MagSafe technology may be Apple-branded, but many Android phone cases support it too. As the headline of our article indicates, we didn't want to write about mounts, wallets, or power banks. Instead, and the goal of this piece was to spotlight "uncommon." We also didn't choose any product that scored less than four stars on Amazon, and we referenced user feedback whenever it was available and applicable.

Today, buying a new CPU requires more than looking at prices, counting cores or choosing the latest model from AMD or Intel. The processor needs to deliver enough performance for the games and programs you use, and it must be compatible with your other components. Without this planning, you may overspend on your CPU and even more on other upgrades. If you're planning to improve the PC you already have, the first step is understanding whether the processor is actually limiting performance. Depending on the situation, it may be more worthwhile to consider upgrading the GPU instead of the CPU, especially depending on the tasks you perform. A better processor helps in several situations, but it does not automatically solve all these problems. Depending on the CPU model you want to buy, this investment may also require new parts to install. Usually, depending on your configuration, the processor may require a new motherboard, memory, or cooler. For that reason, we've narrowed down some of the points to consider before buying a new CPU. Before buying a CPU, the first point to consider is whether it is compatible with the motherboard you currently have in your PC. Even the most powerful processors on the market need a suitable platform to work, since the socket needs to be compatible with the processor. Usually, this varies considerably depending on whether you choose an AMD or Intel CPU. For AMD processors, such as Ryzen, choosing a motherboard is a little easier. The platform currently supports AM4 and AM5, so one is not compatible with the other, but you only have two options. With Intel, this is usually a little more varied, since the company tends to change its processor socket more often. For example, Series 2 Core Ultra processors use LGA1851, which isn't compatible with LGA1700. Still, even if the socket matches your motherboard, it's worth checking the supported CPU list on the manufacturer's website. It shows which processors were validated and the required version for each one, and in some cases, manual updates are necessary. Without them, the computer may not start because of an incompatible BIOS. CPUs, especially flagships, can be very expensive, so before you invest in one, think about what you plan to do on your PC. The best model for you will depend on your particular needs, be it gaming, video editing or rendering, and these may need different characteristics, so the model with the most cores is not always the best for you. It's a good idea to clearly define these priorities before you begin researching your model. For example, if you're buying a CPU for gaming, architecture and cache memory influence performance in addition to core quality alone. Ryzen X3D processors are an excellent option for this segment for exactly that reason, since they use additional cache to accelerate certain workloads. At the same time, some limitations of Ryzen X3D processors make them a less viable option for anyone who wants to focus more on editing. Look for benchmarks of the games and applications you plan to use with your new processor, and check the configuration used in the tests. Also consider the GPU, since if it limits performance, a new CPU won't provide as much gain. If you already have a PC and want to upgrade the CPU, it may be only part of your investment. If you need to change platforms, you'll also need to consider extra expenses, since your budget will mainly need to cover a motherboard. In addition, if you move from a DDR4 processor to DDR5, for example, you also need to buy new RAM. If you don't plan to install these components yourself, you also need to factor in service costs. Once you have all these costs in hand, consider whether it's really worth changing platforms. If another processor option is compatible with your current parts, you can save money by reusing those components. In many cases, making this entire change to your setup for a minimal performance gain is one of the PC upgrades that isn't worth it. For that reason, add everything up and evaluate whether the performance gain justifies the cost. Before buying the CPU, check whether it comes with a cooler and what cooling the manufacturer recommends. If you plan to keep the cooler already in your PC, make sure it is compatible and can handle the demands of the new processor. If the cooler isn't good enough, the CPU may reduce its clock speed to keep temperatures in check, so you might not get the performance you expected from the upgrade. So, if you also plan to switch from air cooling to liquid cooling, consider the processor, budget, and use case. Don't assume every powerful model needs a liquid system, but also don't assume every air cooler will be enough. Research cooler tests with a similar CPU, paying attention to the temperatures other users reach during prolonged tasks, especially if you want to game or render for hours. Also check the available space in the case before choosing the cooling system. Tall heatsinks can prevent the side panel from closing, while certain fans sit over the RAM modules and require adjustments. With liquid systems, check support for the radiator and its fans. Finally, consider airflow, since the cooler needs to work inside a case that can exhaust the heat produced by the components. Replacing a CPU also means checking whether the rest of your PC can support the change, including the power supply. For that reason, evaluate the processor's power consumption alongside the graphics card and other components, leaving headroom for variations and future upgrades. Also check the model's maximum power specifications, since base values don't necessarily reflect its turbo limit. This way, you avoid sizing a power supply based on a number that does not reflect every usage condition. Besides wattage, check the connectors the motherboard requires, especially if you plan to replace it. CPU power uses EPS/ATX12V, and the number of required connections should follow your motherboard manual. If your current power supply already offers enough capacity and the correct cables for the upgrade, replacing the processor doesn't mean you will also need to replace the power supply. However, if it is insufficient for your new specs, you should also upgrade the power supply, since it can damage your PC.

Upgrading a PC is one of the most exciting things a gamer can do, especially if you're finally updating your graphics card. The basic (and oftentimes easiest) choice is picking between an Nvidia and an AMD GPU (the chip itself, like the RX or RTX) — but when you get to different brands of graphics cards themselves, the variety can make your head spin. Why are Nvidia GPUs built by different brands, though? Well, the easiest way to understand it is to follow the lifecycle of a random Nvidia GPU. First, Nvidia designs the chip and puts together a reference card. Referred to as the Founders Edition card, this is essentially the vanilla version that sets the standard hardware specs and serves as a baseline for other manufacturers to follow. From there, the so-called Add-In Board (AIB) partners, such as MSI and Gigabyte, purchase the chips and the core boards, and make their own designs as an offshoot of Nvidia's specification. The AIB partners may, for instance, add extra coolers, RGB lights, a case, and what have you. These companies can even put out factory overclocked Nvidia GPUs to market the product better and slightly bump up the price. This may seem like needless complication, but it actually makes sense from a business perspective. Nvidia only works with the best suppliers and manufacturers, which drastically decreases the risk of being involved in all steps of manufacturing. This has gone on for decades, so it's something all gamers have to accept. Believe it or not, there's no clear-cut answer as to whether a differently branded Nvidia GPU makes any difference. Technically speaking, you're purchasing an identical GPU, so your performance will be quite consistent. Still, there are slight variations between major graphics card manufacturers that might impact your experience. Remember those tweaks that companies make? Some may bump up the VRAM, and others might add an extra fan or opt for a blower-style cooling system, which may be up your alley if you've got a compact case with subpar airflow. It's more about the overall configuration, as the form factor (whether it can even fit inside the case) matters more than aesthetics. There's also the question of reliability. Gamers have their own preferences, and some manufacturers like Asus are considered to have slightly better temperature efficiency. When you look around online, you'll quickly find that certain brands are simply held in higher regard than others. One Reddit user laid it out succinctly by calling Asus and EVGA top-tier, identifying Gigabyte and MSI as your mid-range options, and saying that stuff manufactured by Colorful isn't all that desirable in the community. Other Reddit users generally agreed with this sentiment, especially in terms of Asus being the best. Either way, if you trust the brand and other people aren't complaining about it everywhere you look, you're probably in good hands. Pick the specs you prefer, the right size, and see if the manufacturer's warranty instills some extra trust. And that's pretty much it — no reason to lose sleep over the little stuff.
