TOPICS                      columnists                           OPINION               EU executive branch is building a sovereign backup with Element, not replacing Teams. Not yet anyway      You'd swear from the over-the-top reactions that someone is threatening to take European Commission workers' dogs out back and shoot them. Why the freakout? Because the EC is deploying a self-hosted alternative to Microsoft Teams to keep staff communicating if Microsoft's service becomes unavailable. To be clear, the Commission isn't replacing Teams with Element Pro; it's setting up a backup. That's it. That's all. But according to a Politico report, users are having fits. Element is "absolute shit," rants one. Another proclaims: "The US would 'instantly win the war' if it ever decided to switch off its technology." Uh, guy, that's exactly the point. If US providers cut off European users, whether by choice or government order, many EU governments and companies would face serious disruption. That's exactly why Europe needs an open source, sovereign backup. That's the entire point of this exercise. Take away all the hysteria, and you're left with a rather mundane business-continuity initiative. Don't think for a minute that Trump wouldn't have a snit and order tech giants to block services to officials. Just ask Kimberly Prost, a Canadian International Criminal Court judge, who, besides losing tech services, also lost her credit cards, access to Amazon and Google services. "Alexa wouldn't talk to me," she says – punishment indeed. Now imagine Russia and its allies start attacking the Baltic states. Oh, wait, Putin is already doing that. Then it gets heated, and Trump decides to side with his good friend Putin. What happens to American tech companies' services in Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania? I can answer that in two words: "Nothing good." That said, the EC of course is not dumping Microsoft services. No, it has configured Element Pro to run on the Commission's own infrastructure. An internal memo described the service as an "internal backup" that gives the EU's executive branch an alternative channel for internal messaging, audio and video calls, file transfers, and project discussion rooms. Let me spell it out for you. This is a Commission initiative. It's not an EU-wide order to abandon Microsoft software. I'd love that myself, but that's not what's happening here. Teams will remain the principal platform, while Element provides a fallback intended to reduce dependence on an externally operated communications service. Got it? I hope so! Mind you, there are other good reasons to dump Microsoft Teams. I'm not a fan. For my sins I have to use it and every other groupware program out there. And, I might add, I've been using them since Lotus Notes rolled out the door in 1990.  READ MORE  Digital sovereignty isn't just a good idea. It's essential. Or, as an EC July staff memo put it: "In practice, this means having greater control over our data and systems so that we can reduce risks and limit disruption to our work, wherever possible." Exactly so. Element's architecture is well suited to digital sovereignty. Built on Matrix, an open standard for real-time communications, the platform supports self-hosting, decentralized operation, and interoperability with other Matrix-based systems. Element also supports end-to-end encrypted messaging and calls. You see, the sovereignty argument isn't just about getting an EU-based technology stack. After all, Element is a British company. No, what really makes Element a winner for the EC is that it's mature groupware that lets them deploy and run the system on their own infrastructure rather than relying on Microsoft's cloud. As for the crybaby users, suck it up. No one ever likes change. If the EC switches over to Element lock, stock, and barrel, I suspect much of today's outrage will be forgotten in six months. I've seen this time and time again. Some short-term inconvenience is a reasonable price for greater control over essential communications in an uncertain world. A complete switch isn't the plan now. I think it should be. ® Element told The Register: "Governments and defense organizations are migrating to sovereign alternatives to ensure they can still operate effectively in extreme circumstances. As IT strategy and IT functions move quickly, less adaptive end-users may well feel discomfort as the US Big Tech solutions they've been used to are replaced by sovereign alternatives. Hopefully this is the largest inconvenience most people experience over the coming decade. "We've only had positive and constructive feedback from our actual customers; the leaders and IT functions that are driving sovereignty. "There's inevitably a few unhappy change-resistant users in large deployments, but we work in lockstep with our customers to gather feedback and incorporate it, especially during the trial phase. From what we see in the field, open source alternatives like Element are ready for primetime as a much needed alternative to dependency on the big tech vendors." The Beatles made their first single three separate times in 1962, and on each of those three days a different man was sitting behind the drums. This is not a fan theory anyone had to reconstruct: the liner notes on the band's own Anthology state it flatly that "The Beatles recorded Love Me Do three times in 1962 â on 6 June, and 4 and 11 September 1962 â on each occasion with a different drummer." The first attempt came on Wednesday, June 6, 1962, in Studio Two at EMI's studios on Abbey Road, with Pete Best on the kit. George Martin, the Parlophone A&R man who had agreed to meet the group on the reasoning that he had nothing to lose, got four songs onto tape that night: "Besame Mucho," "Love Me Do," "P.S. I Love You" and "Ask Me Why."  None of the four was released, and only two of them survived in EMI's vaults at all, which meant that the "Love Me Do" recorded that eveningâslower than the one you know, with John Lennon's harmonica opening itâsat unheard by anybody outside the building for the next three decades. Ten weeks later, Best was gone. On the morning of August 16, road manager Neil Aspinall drove him into Liverpool and dropped him in Whitechapel, and at 10 o'clock Brian Epstein delivered the news in his office above the NEMS record shop: "The boys want you out and Ringo in." When Best asked why, Epstein gave him two reasons, and they were the same reason twice. "They don't think you're a good enough drummer, Pete," he said. "And George Martin doesn't think you're a good enough drummer." Ringo Starr's first session with the band came on September 4, by which point the contract was signedâ"By this time we did have a contract," Paul McCartney said laterâand the group put down around fifteen takes of the backing track. Martin made one call in the room that outlasted the day: Lennon could not sing the words "love me do" with a harmonica in his mouth, so the line went to McCartney, and his nervousness at being handed it is audible on the finished record. A week after that, Martin hired a professional. Andy White, a session drummer already booked for the date, was at Abbey Road when the Beatles turned up on September 11, and Ringoâfour weeks into the jobâwas handed a tambourine and told to shake it. White was paid a flat fee of Â£5 15s, collected no royalties then or ever, and barely registered the man he had displaced.  "Ringo and I didn't have much between us, all my time was taken up learning the routines, and he was playing the tambourines so he was only there for the take," he told the Daily Record. The Beatles' own Anthology notes that the substitution "came as quite a shock" to the band and especially to Ringo, and that it was the only time in the group's career that he was replaced this way. Both September recordings went out on records: when Parlophone released "Love Me Do" backed with "P.S. I Love You" on October 5, 1962, the label was red, and the drummer was Ringo. Later pressings switched to a black label and carried the September 11 recording with White on drums, and that is also the version on the Please Please Me album. The tambourine is the tell, because it is not on the September 4 take at all: hear one, and you are hearing Ringo play the drums; hear the other, and he is standing off to the side keeping time on a piece of jingling tin.  The single reached No. 17 in Britain, which Aspinall thought was no small thingâ"They'd sold a lot of records for 'Love Me Do' to get to Number Seventeen, which was great for a Liverpool band â they'd made the charts!" Best's version turned up in 1994 and was released for the first time on Anthology 1 on November 20, 1995. Sneak leek. A GTA 6 leaker has reportedly threatened to put out a complete, playable build of the game, start to finish. The threat was posted on CyberLeek's website after the leaker shared 25 minutes of footage from the game earlier this week. Rockstar has previously issued statements regarding the leaker, noting that the leaks are "heartbreaking" and that "this is obviously not how we intended for you to see the game after all this time". Take-Two, Rockstar's parent company, has been hunting for the person behind the leaks, and has tried to subpoena Discord for information pertaining to the leaker's identity. After going quiet for a bit, CyberLeek came back with a bang this week, posting new footage from Rockstar's upcoming game that even features nude scenes, including a fully naked Jason, and a topless Lucia. Eurogamer has seen the video, and it appears to be legitimate - and, as is now traditional, has CyberLeek's emblem overlaid on top of the footage. CyberLeek now reportedly says the build will go out if their cryptocurrency coin reaches a market cap of $30 million, and claims it can be played through to the end credits. "Here's the deal, nice and clean," the demand reads. "CyberLeek hits 30 million marketcap, the build goes out — full story mode, played to the end, credits and all. Don't believe it has full story mode? Ask for what you want to see, and it gets provided. Take-Two gets one way out: physical disks and a public apology. They can take it at any moment. Or they can gamble that CL is bluffing. Everyone knows which one they'll pick." GTA 6 is due out on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S on 19th November. Japanese convenience stores could begin employing humanoid robots as early as 2027, with new AI-powered machines capable of stocking shelves, managing inventory, bagging purchases and assisting customers in more than 20 languages. The technology was showcased at an international retail industry event in Tokyo on October 8, attended by representatives from 18 countries and more than 30 companies. Among the exhibits was the C1 humanoid robot, developed by CP AI Robotics, a company operating primarily in Thailand. Unlike conventional industrial robots that follow predetermined instructions, the C1 uses physical AI to recognize products, interpret its surroundings and perform tasks in environments shared with human employees and customers. The robot can transport merchandise, replenish store shelves, manage inventory and package purchased items. It can also communicate with customers in over 20 languages, using facial expressions and gestures to make interactions more natural. CP AI Robotics plans to begin full-scale deployment of the C1 in Japanese convenience stores as early as 2027, potentially introducing one or more robots per location. The company believes the technology could help address Japan’s ongoing labor shortages, particularly in convenience stores where employees must handle numerous responsibilities throughout the day and night. Weidong Sun of CP AI Robotics explained that robots could reduce employees’ workloads while also improving security during nighttime operations. However, the company emphasized that its goal is not to eliminate human workers:  “We basically want to provide services in an environment where robots work alongside people. We are not aiming for completely unmanned stores. We believe the human touch is absolutely essential. We hope to contribute to solving Japan’s labor shortage.”  The company envisions robots handling repetitive and physically demanding tasks while human employees remain responsible for customer relationships and duties requiring personal judgment. The October 2025 crypto crash exposed the dangers of leverage and crowded bets. A year later, analysts say those risks remain. Nearly a year after one of crypto's most violent selloffs, the question hanging over the market is whether traders have learned enough to prevent another one. Just days after hitting a record high above $126,000O, on October 10, 2025, bitcoin BTC$82,800.62 plunged from around $122,000 to $105,000, with much of the decline occurring within minutes. The crash triggered roughly $19 billion in liquidations across crypto markets, catching traders off guard after months of bets on further gains. But while the selloff shook confidence in the market, the conditions that helped cause it haven't gone away. "It just was a very quick and violent market top that we did not expect," said Mark Connors of Risk Dimensions, who previously ran a hedge fund positioning product at Credit Suisse. "Positioning was important then, and it's important today," he said in an interview. Coming into the crash, open interest was near historic highs, and traders had piled into bullish positions, betting that bitcoin would follow its familiar four-year cycle toward fresh records. "People were keenly aware, like me, they were bulled up because it was 'go' time," Connors said. "We were going to go to that $250,000 to $300,000, $400,000 level using previous cycles." Instead, the market turned against them. "The movement was obviously not onchain data. I mean, it was all derivatives," he said. "So paper bitcoin again is alive and well and governs the near term." The lesson, he argues, is that bitcoin's price can be driven as much by leveraged bets as by demand for the asset itself. That hasn't changed much in the past year. Perpetual futures, which allow traders to bet on price moves without owning bitcoin, remain a major part of crypto trading. Exchanges also have strong financial incentives to keep offering leveraged products. Still, traders may be better equipped to navigate the risks. "The data is getting better at defining what the market structure is," Connors argued, pointing to improved visibility into order books and positioning. "More information means greater certainty, less volatility." Chris Sullivan, co-founder of Hyperion Decimus, said traders can take steps to protect themselves from the kind of losses seen last October. His advice starts with avoiding leverage and keeping a close eye on open interest, funding rates and market sentiment. Open interest tracks the number of outstanding derivatives contracts, while funding rates reflect the cost of holding positions in perpetual futures. Together, they can help traders spot when the market is leaning too far in one direction. Sullivan also urged patience when those measures reach extremes, whether traders are betting on rising or falling prices. For long-term bitcoin holders, he recommended buying the asset, moving it off exchanges and holding it in self-custody rather than leaving it with a trading platform. That doesn't mean another crash is off the table. "There's still a chance that you can have an October 10th for sure," Connors warned. "The levered products have not gone away." The crash also challenged one of bitcoin's most widely held assumptions: that its four-year cycle, tied to the halving of mining rewards, could serve as a reliable guide to future prices. "We all, including me, got caught offside," Connors said. "The four-year cycle is not dead; it has changed, and we can't rely on it for as much signal as we have in the past." He now believes economic and political forces may play a larger role in bitcoin's cycles than investors once thought. Meanwhile, the growth of institutional investment products has done little to displace the derivatives market's influence over short-term prices. For all the changes since October 2025, Connors sees one important distinction between the crash and its aftermath. "I think a year later, we learned to be more attentive to market structure," he said. And despite the damage, bitcoin's market survived. "The market did bend; it didn't break." Lucknow brides can no longer afford traditional silver nagras Save Share In Lucknow, the capital of Uttar Pradesh and a city known for its Nawabi heritage and artisanship, 55-year-old Azhar Hussain sits at the bench where he has spent years making decorative footwear. His tools are still there, but the customers are not. Amid soaring silver prices over the past year, demand for his work has plummeted. The small workshop sits beside Chowk Bazaar, one of Old Lucknow’s oldest and busiest markets, a famed hub for wedding shopping full of silver jewellery and handcrafts. For three decades, Hussain has been one of the bazaar’s busiest craftsmen, making a distinctive form of silver slip-on shoes, known locally as nagras. He starts by cutting a thin silver sheet into the outline of a nagra, then sketches floral and leaf motifs onto the metal. Hussain then rests the sheet on heated lac, a soft natural resin that cushions the metal while he uses a hammer and engraving tool to tap intricate designs into place. Hussain then bends the silver around a foot-shaped furma, or mould, before fitting it over a base of cardboard, rubber and velvet, soldering the pieces together and polishing the pair. Craftsmen have used this process to make silver nagras since the 1600s. Originally, the decorative shoes were made for daily use by the Nawabi, Muslim rulers of the former kingdom of Awadh. “Silver nagras used to be the most important part of a nawab’s attire,” said 68-year-old Nawab Masud Abdullah, an eighth-generation descendant of Nawab Muhammad Ali Shah, the ninth Nawab of Awadh, who ruled from 1837 until he died in 1842. “They were not just footwear; they represented our culture and heritage,” he added. Once reserved exclusively for Nawabs, silver nagras have become a cherished wedding tradition over the last century, embraced by Lucknow’s middle and upper classes alike. “Our forefathers wore silver nagras every day. Later, they became reserved for celebrations and eventually only for special occasions,” Abdullah explained. “The good thing was that the tradition spread beyond the Nawabs. People, particularly brides across Lucknow, embrace it as their own and now a bride is considered incomplete without a nagra.”   Hussain and his family of craftsmen have seen this transformation firsthand. “In the past, only Nawabs could afford these shoes because they symbolised wealth, power and status,” he said. “But over the last seven or eight decades, they became popular among middle-class and wealthy families too, especially for weddings and special occasions.” There are two types of silver nagras — open-toed chappals and closed-toed jutis, and customers can choose different patterns, ornamentation and designs.  Hussain’s family has been making nagras since the early 1900s and the trade has provided a comfortable living. Before each wedding season, he has typically made about 10 pairs a month, he says, with each priced between $105 and $230 (10,000 and 22,000 rupees). “We lived with dignity,” he said quietly. “We earned enough to feed our family, educate our children and save a little every month. We never imagined that one day we would struggle even to run our household.” Over the past year, however, the orders have vanished with the rise in silver prices. The metal was already costing a bit more before the U.S.-Iran war launched in February, owing to tight supplies and growing investor demand. But the conflict added another jolt, as uncertainty in global markets drove investors towards silver and put the metal — and the nagras — out of reach for many Lucknow shoppers.  Prices for precious metals actually began rising with Russia’s invasion of Ukraine back in early 2022, but economists say prices surged significantly with the US and Israeli attacks on Iran. In 2023, silver prices in India largely fluctuated between $725 (70,000 rupees) and $830 (80,000 rupees) per kilogramme, rising to around $985 (98,000 rupees) in 2024. But this year, amid the conflict with Iran, silver prices briefly soared as high as $4,670 (450,000 rupees) per kg before easing after the ceasefire. Even now, after some decline, prices are hovering around $2,600 (250,000 rupees) per kg, more than three times their levels just a few years ago. Dr. Salahuddin Ayyub, an economist and international trade expert with India’s Ministry of Commerce and Industry, said geopolitical conflicts have triggered unprecedented volatility in global commodity markets. “When stock markets become volatile, investors move their money into safer assets, such as gold and silver,” Ayyub explained. “This sudden surge in demand pushes the prices of precious metals sharply upwards.” The consequences have been particularly severe in India, he said, because gold and silver remain deeply intertwined with weddings, other cultural traditions and family savings. As prices continue to rise, many households are increasingly opting for lower-cost alternatives, such as artificial jewellery. He warned that while consumers may find substitutes, those whose livelihoods depend on the precious metals industry, including artisans, silversmiths, jewellery shopkeepers and traditional craftsmen, have far fewer options. “The impact extends well beyond consumers,” Ayyub said. “Entire communities whose incomes depend on these metals are now facing shrinking demand and growing economic uncertainty.” The surge in silver prices has had another consequence that is often overlooked by the government and policymakers. According to Ayyub, when a country witnesses a sharp rise in demand for imported precious metals, governments often intervene to curb imports and protect their foreign exchange reserves. “India depends heavily on imported silver. A sudden spike in imports puts pressure on the country’s foreign exchange reserves, so the government tries to discourage excessive imports through tariffs and other restrictions,” Ayyub said. These import duties are eventually passed on to consumers. “As tariffs increase, the landed cost of silver rises. That is one of the reasons why silver prices in India are currently trading above global prices,” he said. Globally, silver currently costs $2,100 (201,000 rupees) per kg, but in India, it’s more than 20 percent higher because of heavy government import taxes and strict licensing that chokes off supply. India depends on imports to meet more than 80% of its domestic silver demand and its purchases account for over 20 percent of the global trade in refined silver. India more than doubled its effective import taxes on gold and silver in May. That saw silver imports plunge by 87 percent to just $75.6 million that month, down from $566.2 million the previous year, the country’s lowest level in over three years. High silver prices are now forcing Lucknow’s brides to make tough, sometimes devastating, decisions.  For 28-year-old Lucknow resident Uzma Siddique, who is set to marry in December, owning and wearing a pair of silver nagras on her big day has always topped her wedding wishlist. “My mother wore silver nagras at her wedding in 1992. So did my grandmother and so did my great-grandmother,” Siddique said. “I always imagined myself wearing them and taking my wedding photographs in them and posting them on Instagram. It was never just footwear; it was an emotion and a family tradition.” But when she visited the market with plans to order a pair, the prices stunned her. “A pair that cost around $156 to $208 (15,000 to 20,000 rupees) just a few years ago is now selling for nearly $673 (65,000 rupees),” she said. Determined to have a pair, she decided to give up on other wedding luxuries instead. “I had to cut back on many other wedding expenses. I bought a lighter lehenga (long skirt), reduced the number of suits I planned to purchase, and trimmed my budget in several places, just so I could afford these nagras.” Despite the financial strain, she says giving up the footwear tradition was never an option. “They have become incredibly expensive, but our emotions are attached to them. That’s why I still bought them,” she said. But many of her friends have had to go without. “Some had dreamed of wearing silver nagras on their wedding day, but they had to let go of that dream because they simply couldn’t afford them. They are deeply hurt by it,” she said. Not far from Siddique’s home lives her friend, 25-year-old Safiya Khan, who is also getting married in December. Unlike Siddique, Safiya has not been able to buy silver nagras for her wedding. From a lower middle-class family, she says soaring prices put upholding that tradition out of reach. “My entire wedding shopping budget is around $1,250 (120,000 rupees). I simply cannot spend more than half of it on a pair of shoes,” Khan said, noting that she was sad to end the family tradition. “I think this tradition will end with my generation,” she said. “My mother had a pair of silver nagras, but she had to sell them last year because of financial difficulties. We always believed we would buy another pair for my wedding. Had we known silver prices would rise so dramatically, we would never have sold them.” She has been shocked by how a distant war has so negatively affected this beloved local tradition. “I know the recent conflicts have pushed silver prices higher, but I never imagined that a war thousands of km away could take away a tradition so close to my heart,” she said. “I had always dreamed of taking my wedding photographs in silver nagras. Now that dream will never come true.”  Naseem Jahan, a Lucknow resident in her late seventies, still treasures the pair of silver chappals her mother gave her for her wedding in 1972. “I remember my mother paid around $2.50 (250 rupees) for this pair,” Jahan recalled. “We had to wait nearly seven months after placing the order before it was finally ready. Those were beautiful days.” More than five decades later, the silver slippers remain one of her most cherished possessions. She has them polished every three years and proudly wears them to weddings and other important family gatherings, as do many of the older women in Lucknow. “Every time I wear them, people come to admire them and praise their beauty. That makes me so happy,” she said with a smile. But Jahan fears the tradition may not continue into the next generation. “Today, very few people can afford such footwear,” she said. When she recently visited the market to buy a similar pair for her granddaughter, the soaring price of silver made it unaffordable. Still, she wants her granddaughter to have traditional bridal footwear, so she has made a tough decision. “I have decided to gift her my own pair,” she said. “Let these slippers adorn her feet now. I want them to continue their journey.” As the only precious keepsake she has preserved from her wedding, Jahan knows how connected brides feel to the shoes. “I have developed an emotional bond with them. They remind me of my mother, my wedding day and the Lucknow I grew up in. I only wish silver prices would come down again so that more people could experience this tradition.” Jahan’s decision to part with her silver nagras will keep a pair in her family, but it will not bring new work to the craftsmen who once made the footwear for Lucknow’s brides. In Chowk Bazaar, dwindling demand has left many artisans facing the prospect of a trade that may not survive long enough to serve the next generation.  Jabbar Hussain, 48, a fourth-generation craftsman and shopkeeper who makes nagras and sells them in his shop, sits in his empty store in Lucknow’s Chowk Bazaar, struggling to understand what has happened to a business that once flourished. Between June and September, Hussain’s shop would normally be crowded with customers placing orders for nagras. But over the past three months, Hussain says, he has not sold a single pair. He blames the unprecedented rise in silver prices for making the handmade footwear a luxury few can now afford. “A pair that once sold for around $125 (12,000 rupees) now costs between $622 and $778 (60,000 and 75,000 rupees) because silver has become so expensive,” he said. “People still walk into the shop, admire the craftsmanship and ask about the price. But the moment they hear it, they quietly leave. Every customer who walks away feels like another piece of our family's future disappearing.” Hussain, like others before him, now fears he will be forced to close his shop. “There were nearly 30 of us not long ago,” he said. “Most have already abandoned the profession because silver has become too expensive and orders have dried up. Those who are still here are also thinking of leaving.” He is now thinking of taking a loan to open a cafe, which he hopes will provide a steady income. “I need to find another way to earn,” he said. Hussain had hoped to teach the craft to his sons so they could carry forward the family’s legacy, but now he is advising them to pursue other professions. He no longer sees a future in the silver nagras trade and blames the war in the Middle East. “We have nothing to do with this war, yet we are paying the price,” he said, frustrated at how a conflict so far away has threatened his livelihood. “I don’t know what our future looks like anymore. Sometimes I think about what will happen to this craft and I cry. This wasn’t just our profession; it was our identity, our heritage and everything we were known for.”  Still, Hussain clings to the hope that silver prices will decline and orders will return. Economists and market analysts are less optimistic. Ayyub said silver prices are expected to remain above $2,085 per  (200,000 rupees) kg for the foreseeable future because once precious metal prices rise sharply, they rarely fall significantly enough to return to their previous levels. Historically, the same has been the case with gold. “Even if prices decline, they are unlikely to return to their earlier levels,” Ayyub said. Not far from Hussain’s workshop, 40-year-old former silver nagras maker Kuldeep Gautam now spends his days behind the counter of a jewellery shop. Known for his intricate workmanship, Gautam once earned between $415 and $518 (40,000 and 50,000 rupees) a month making the ornate footwear. But he has not received a single order since January, he says. As orders disappeared and his savings dwindled, Gautam was forced to abandon the craft and take up a job as a salesman. “I left the craft because I had no other choice,” he said. “Whenever I pass my old workshop, I don’t even look at it. It hurts too much.” Beyond the loss of income, Kuldeep says he mourns the loss of the identity his craft had given him. “People knew me for my work and appreciated my craftsmanship. It gave me dignity. Today, I earn only $155 (15,000 rupees) a month, and I struggle to pay my children’s school fees. I never imagined my life would come to this.” “I still yearn to make nagras, but there are no buyers anymore. The war has destroyed our lives.” Back in his shop, Azhar Hussain also faces the prospect of abandoning a craft that has carried his family for more than a century. His plan, he says, is to secure a bank loan to buy an electric rickshaw so he can start earning again. “At least an e-rickshaw will earn me $5 to $7 (500 to 700 rupees) a day,” he said. “I don’t want to leave this craft, but I have no choice.” Follow Al Jazeera English:

Tokenized commodities could grow from a market dominated by gold into a broader system for financing metals, trading energy and borrowing against physical assets, according to executives at Paxos Labs, Theo and Energy Substantiation. Putting commodities on blockchain networks should do more than make them easier to buy, the executives say. It could connect investors seeking exposure and income with businesses that need inventory financing, opening markets traditionally reserved for large institutions. The starting point remains modest. Tokenized commodities’ market capitalization reached $5.55 billion at the end of March 2026, up from $1.43 billion at the beginning of 2025, according to CoinGecko. Gold-backed tokens from Paxos and Tether accounted for almost 90% of that growth. Tokenized commodities are blockchain-based tokens that represent ownership of, or exposure to, physical assets such as gold, silver and oil. Paxos Labs is betting that lending can unlock the next stage. Its PAXGy token is backed by PAX Gold PAXG$4,185.84, with reserves deployed to institutional borrowers. Each token is designed to become redeemable for more PAXG as underlying lending rates are paid back in ounce terms, allowing holders to potentially increase their gold holdings while retaining price exposure. “The big proposition is access,” co-founder Bhau Kotecha told CoinDesk in an interview. Gold lending has historically required scale and relationships unavailable to many investors, he said. Kotecha sees demand from individuals, family offices and institutions, with borrowing against PAXGy a possible next step. Lending returns are not guaranteed, and borrower defaults could erode the token’s value. Silver offers another route into that financing market. Theo’s thSLVR product passes income from institutional silver leases to holders while maintaining exposure to the metal’s price. Theo Chief Investment Officer Iggy Ioppe sees growth coming from existing commodity owners and users: institutions seeking productive collateral, refiners financing inventory and corporate treasuries seeking assets that settle quickly. Silver is “the natural second” after gold, he said, citing industrial demand and an established leasing market, although greater volatility and a tighter supply of available metal complicate the opportunity. Ioppe forecasts a tokenized commodities market worth tens of billions within five years and more than $100 billion within a decade. Within 15 years, he expects tokenization to become part of ordinary commodity settlement and financing. Oil presents a larger logistical challenge, and, in EnSub’s view, a substantial opportunity. The company expanded its WTIC token from Ethereum to Solana on Oct. 2. Each token represents one barrel of West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude backed by verified physical inventory, according to its announcement. Co-founder and CEO JP Thieriot said natural gas and Brent tokens are under development. He expects demand from energy buyers hedging costs, investors seeking exposure and suppliers needing working capital, predicting oil tokens could account for a quarter of the oil market within 10 years. The executives differ on how quickly energy can follow metals. Ioppe argued that storage and transport make income-generating energy tokens harder to build. Thieriot said “verifiable inventory, workable custody and settlement” are essential for commodities continuously in motion. Expansion will therefore depend on connecting tokens to reliable physical markets, and giving owners a compelling reason to use them. Tech is driving the economy, and investments are flowing in. But food costs are rising and debt is growing, making the economy a concern for many voters. Save Share After three years of Israel’s multi-front war in the Middle East, it would be no surprise if this month’s Knesset elections were taking place against the backdrop of an economy in dire straits. Instead, Israel’s economy is – by many measures – flourishing.     After slowing sharply in the initial aftermath of the Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attacks and Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, Israel has rebounded to become one of the fastest-growing advanced economies in recent years. Gross domestic product (GDP) grew 2.9 percent in 2025, picking up from a 1 percent expansion in 2024, and 3.2 percent in the first half of this year, according to government figures. The Bank of Israel has forecast 4 percent growth for the whole of 2026 and 5.5 percent growth in 2027 – projections that far exceed the outlooks for major economies such as the United States, United Kingdom, France, Canada, and Japan. Over the past three years, the shekel has strengthened against the US dollar, hitting a three-decade high in May, and Israel’s stock market has surged, with the benchmark TA-125 up more than 110 percent. Meanwhile, unemployment stands at 2.8 percent, while inflation is modest at 1.5 percent. Against this relatively rosy economic backdrop, campaigning for the October 27 election has been dominated by national security, with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, leader of the right-wing Likud party, and retired general Gadi Eisenkot, head of the centrist Yashar, each claiming to be most qualified to keep Israelis safe. Driving Israel’s striking economic resilience has been a booming tech sector largely insulated from its conflicts spanning Gaza, Lebanon, Syria, Iraq, Iran and Yemen. Despite being on a war footing since October 2023, Israel has attracted record levels of investment in tech, the driver of about one-fifth of economic activity, amid the frenetic global rollout of artificial intelligence (AI). Total direct foreign investment hit a record $26.2bn last year, up 78 percent from 2024, led by US tech giants Alphabet and Palo Alto Networks’ record-breaking acquisitions of Israeli cybersecurity firms Wiz and CyberArk, respectively. Foreign capital has continued to flood into the country this year, with inflows reaching a quarterly record of $14.1bn in the January-March period, according to government figures. Along with prospering from the global AI boom, Israel’s tech scene has benefitted from its close ties to the local defence sector, which has ramped up orders from hundreds of startups supplying everything from radar systems to communications platforms and anti-drone technology. While Israel’s economy has bounced back in part due to robust employment and wage growth, its resilience is primarily an “export-driven story that reflects strong global technology demand, particularly in areas where Israel – and multinational firms operating from Israel – is globally competitive, such as cybersecurity and artificial intelligence,” said Keren Uziyel, a senior analyst for the Middle East and Africa at the Economist Intelligence Unit (EIU). “Interest in Israel’s technology goods and services is driving high levels of FDI and venture capital fundraising, and boosting the capital markets, which in turn is having significant wealth effects and boosting government revenue,” Uziyel told Al Jazeera. But Israel’s military campaigns have come at an enormous cost to the public purse. In March, the Bank of Israel estimated that Israel’s war costs to date had reached approximately 350 billion shekels ($114.6bn) – a figure not including the then recently-launched Iran war. Military expenditures are on track to rise substantially in the coming years as Israeli leaders double down on “national security”. Netanyahu, whose right-wing coalition has cast security as “the foundation of everything else”, has pushed to raise the annual defence budget to 183 billion shekels ($60bn), equivalent to roughly 9 percent of GDP. If passed, the budget would raise military spending by two and a half times what it was before October 7. Outgoing opposition leader Yair Lapid has backed an expanded defence budget, but has clashed with Netanyahu about how to fund it. Though security has dominated the run-up to the election, opinion polling suggests that Israelis also view the economy as a key concern. In an opinion poll released by the Israel Democracy Institute last month, 38 percent of Jewish Israelis and 46 percent of Palestinian citizens of Israel – who make up about 20 percent of the population – chose the economy and the cost of living as the most important or second-most important election issue. Israel’s high cost of living, in particular, has long been a source of public discontent. Israel has for years ranked among the most expensive countries in the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), a dynamic economists attribute to the country’s limited trade relations with its neighbours and cumbersome regulations. Though Israel’s overall rate of inflation has been modest, food prices have risen at a faster pace, increasing 8 percent between the start of 2024 and mid-2026, according to consumer advocacy group Lobby 99. “People are worried about the economy but not so much about the macroeconomic situation, more so on their personal perspectives, especially cost of living,” Ayal Kimhi, vice president of the Shoresh Institution for Socioeconomic Research in Tel Aviv, told Al Jazeera. “However, the security situation dominates the public discourse for obvious reasons, so I do not think the economy will play a major role in the vote,” Kimhi said. “Some parties do not even bother presenting a vision or an agenda,” he added. “Other parties do not differ much about economic issues.” While Israel’s headline economic figures are impressive, they come with caveats attached. Economists note that while Israel’s economy has grown much faster than its peers, GDP has been boosted in part by the country’s usually high population growth, which has averaged nearly 2 percent over the past decade. Israel’s growth trajectory has also taken a hit despite the expansion, with the Bank of Israel estimating an accumulated loss of output through the end of 2025 equivalent to 8.6 percent of annual GDP. Joseph Zeira, a professor of economics at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, said the country’s economic performance has “not been great at all” considering that growth has consistently lagged the pre-conflict trend since late 2023. “Actual living standards depend on the area,” Zeira told Al Jazeera, adding that Israelis are grappling with “higher prices, or rather lower real wages and incomes”, and deteriorating public services. “The only improvement is some decline in housing prices due to a vast wave of construction in recent years,” he said. The long-term health of Israel’s public finances is another concern. While Israel’s debt-to-GDP ratio of about 68 is far below that of peers such as the US, the UK, France, and Italy, the gap between government revenue and spending has grown rapidly over the past three years. In its latest annual report, the Bank of Israel said it was “essential” for the government to “restore orderly budgetary processes” and implement “credible measures” to reduce the public debt. Other long-term challenges include boosting labour participation among ultra-Orthodox Jewish men – whose refusal to do military service has become a major election issue – and Arab women (among Palestinian citizens of Israel), both of whom are employed at much lower rates than the general population. “The cost of the military campaigns and mobilisation has severely strained public finances,” Omer Moav, a professor of economics at the University of Warwick and at Reichman University, told Al Jazeera. “Deficits and national debt have expanded significantly, making current spending trajectories unsustainable without fiscal consolidation,” Moav said. “The next government is facing a huge challenge.” Regardless of who prevails in the election, economists say, Israel’s economic prospects will in large part hinge on whether conflict in the region escalates or subsides. “We expect growth to reach around 4 percent in 2026 and to exceed this level in 2027,” said Uziyel, the EIU analyst. “However, significant downside risks to growth remain should conflicts in Gaza, Iran, or on the Lebanon front resume.” “The outlook depends greatly on the security situation,” said Kimhi of the Shoresh Institution for Socioeconomic Research. “If we are able to put an end to the war and reduce military spending, the future could be bright.”          Follow Al Jazeera English:

Nvidia may be worth $5.6 trillion, but its employees still have to pay up at the company cafeteria. The chipmaker fueling the AI boom, led by CEO Jensen Huang, is the most valuable company in the world by market cap, towering above other tech giants like Google, Apple, and Amazon. But that doesn’t mean the company is giving away free lunch. Gergely Orosz, a software engineer and author of The Pragmatic Engineer newsletter, highlighted Nvidia’s food policies in a June thread on X after a visit to the company’s Santa Clara, Calif., headquarters. “Snacks and coffee are not free: You have to pay for them. This would be unusual at Big Tech, but no big deal for devs here,” Orosz wrote in a post.  Former employees who spoke to Business Insider clarified the company’s cafeteria meals are subsidized, not free. While coffee is generally free, employees must pay for some bottled drinks and drinks from on-site cafés.  The company’s food policies have reportedly been around for more than a decade. A blog by a former intern who worked at Nvidia in 2014 shows even then the food at Nvidia was subsidized, not free, and averaged about $6, or about $8.50 today. Some food options in 2014 included chicken and pasta, chicken and rice, fish and chips, and sandwiches. Nvidia did not immediately respond to Fortune’s request for comment. It’s unclear exactly what’s on the menu today, but posts on Instagram and TikTok show items like bagels, sushi, açai bowls, sandwiches, and omelettes. Other options include butter chicken, ramen, pizza, and a full salad bar. A  job posting shared by Nvidia’s head of culinary operations Jacob Anaya read: “you won’t find our managers referring to a corporate recipe book or our chefs microwaving the lunch special. We do not have standardized recipes or central commissaries, instead, our chefs and managers are expected to stay abreast of current culinary trends and bring cutting edge food into their cafes.” A post shared by Vicky Phu | Bay Area Food Bae 🌿 (@phuoodwithvicks)  Nvidia’s food policy stands apart from other tech companies of its size. The most notable among them is Google, which helped kick off the trend of lavish employee perks that for years have defined tech workplaces. Unlike Nvidia, Google provides free breakfast, lunch, and dinner at cafeterias across its offices. Its Googleplex headquarters in Mountain View, Calif., reportedly has about 30 locations for employees to grab a bite to eat.  Yet at Google, the food is secondary to the connections that come from communion, according to Ruth Porat, the chief investment officer of Google and parent company Alphabet. She said its stocked “micro-kitchens” filled with treats and snacks are located throughout the office to help connect employees from different departments who wouldn’t otherwise speak regularly. “Serendipity is really valuable, and so having people come for meals is one way you get people from all around the company working on different things, all of a sudden comparing ideas,” Porat said during an interview from June.  Nvidia, for its part, is more focused on giving employees better work-life balance through a hybrid work program and no return-to-office mandate than it is on giving them free food, HR director Febe Punsalan previously told Fortune. The company’s approach also reflects its founder’s philosophy. Huang cofounded Nvidia in 1993 and has transformed it from a fledgling video game chipmaker to the engine behind the AI revolution. The CEO works seven days a week and has previously said he is fueled to work so hard by the fear Nvidia could go out of business, even after it has become the most valuable company on the planet. “You know the phrase ‘30 days from going out of business,’ I’ve used for 33 years,” Huang said in an interview with podcast host Joe Rogan last year. “But the feeling doesn’t change. The sense of vulnerability, the sense of uncertainty, the sense of insecurity—it doesn’t leave you.” Huang’s dedication to the grind also reflects his advice to young people. In an address to Stanford students in 2024, he said: “I wish upon you ample doses of pain and suffering.” He argued being uncomfortable often leads to the best results. The era of unlimited free food in Silicon Valley may be nearing its end. In 2024 Meta fired two dozen employees it said were abusing the vouchers. Twitter, now X, was once famous for its gourmet cafeteria with a new menu every day, but many food options were cut back after Elon Musk bought the company in 2022. Still, it’s hard to argue with Nvidia’s approach. While other companies have spent millions to keep employees fed, Nvidia has offered its employees a different, but lucrative, perk: the chance to buy company stock at discounted prices. With the stock rising more than 1,000% in the past five years, its safe to say employees who have held on to their stock have secured much more value from Nvidia than a free lunch. I was set to hate it. I felt I had to. It was made in China, and while I think CFMoto, on general principles, makes pretty good bikes, what business does it have attempting an in-line four? That engine configuration is the stuff of legend. The Chinese want to splash in that pond, they wanna bring their A-game. The SR-S was indeed an in-line four, and I’d sharpened my fangs on in-line fours back when they breathed fire, hailed Satan, and tank-slapped their way to red-line. I kept riding in-line fours after the Japanese engineered the tank-slapping out of them, and their unique shriek will always be one of the great songs of my people. Nothing assaults your ears and screams “Fast” like an in-line four being hammered through the gears. It all began in 1969 with the Honda CB750-Four, the bike that started the so-called superbike era. The prototype was unveiled in 1968 at the Tokyo Motor Show, and the first production bikes arrived in the USA the following year. Kawasaki upped the ante when it unveiled its 900cc Z1 in 1972…and away we all went. In-line fours got bigger, went a hell of a lot faster, and schooled several generations of riders in sheer terror, while simultaneously addicting them to industrial doses of adrenaline. And jail. Around the turn of the century, it was decided that 1000cc was kinda the right capacity for an in-line four superbike, and while Suzuki flirted with a 1400cc in-line four from 2011 to 2008, that fat bastard was never a contender for the superbike crown. Suzuki was alright about that. It also produced what many still believe to be the finest in-line four ever made – the K5-engined GSX-R1000 – which was itself the obvious performance progression of the just-as-legendary GSX-R750, the bike that defined “handling” 25 years ago. Suzuki figured it would just jam its 1000cc monster engine into that wickedly agile 750cc bastard to see if it danced. It did. But to many people, the GSX-R750 still danced just that little bit better. The 1000 went harder, but the 750 handled sharper. That was the argument. And the argument was ultimately settled by the market. Suzuki stopped making the GSX-R750 in 2016, but it was essentially the same bike it had made in 2011. The GSX-R750 was still being sold in the USA up until 2019, but that was just unsold 2016 stock. The in-line 1000 had won out. Size mattered, it seemed. But ask anyone who has ever ridden the GSX-R750 and the GSX-R1000 which one handled better, and they will tell you it was the 750. It was always the 750. We now live in a world where in-line fours are all 1000cc track monsters, and the market all seems to be about parallel twins – the sensible cardigan of the motorcycle world. Older riders, who once sold important organs to buy in-line fours, are now too old and too scared to even care what 14,000rpm in top means on an in-line four. Younger riders are far too risk-averse and have been bludgeoned by legislation and the policing that goes with it to even think about red-lining an in-line four in all six gears. So why the Hell would CFMoto produce an all-new four-cylinder in-line 750? It was going great guns with its parallel twin offerings. They were incredible bang-for-your buck, improving with each model run, and absolutely making the big Japanese Four sit up and pay attention. Why this four-cylinder winged thing, with its strange rear wheel, and cutting-edge suite of electronic whizz-bangery? No idea, and I could care less. Maybe the Chinese are just throwing this 750 SR-S out there to see what would happen. Maybe they wanted to make the Japanese crazy. Maybe it was a little of both. Utkarsh was very kind when he first wrote about this bike, but then Utkarsh is young, full of hope, open of mind and burdened with a sweet disposition. I am not, and I was determined to hate it.  And then I saw it in the flesh and thought: that’s not too bad, actually. Sure, the rear wheel looks like it’s meant to slice giant potatoes, but close inspection revealed those munted inserts could be removed with an Allen key and thrown into the sea. The rest of it looked cool. Very cool. But I was certain it was not going to be a GSX-R750 when I rode it. And I was right. It was not. It was a very long way away from Suzuki’s epic sportsbike statement. CFMoto’s SR-S is a very different statement. Sure, you hit the starter button and it instantly fires into that intoxicating angry beehive hum only an in-line four can make. I remember looking at it after I started it up and muttering: “Well, you certainly sound like you mean business…” And it did, but it was a different kind of business. It was a business for our time. A gentler, friendlier, easier-to-ride kinda business, because we live in just such a world – or we’d like to. Or the government would like us to. So the SR-S is not the GSX-R. For starters, there is no racer’s crouch happening here. You sit canted forward, but not in a way that puts all your weight on your arms and forces your neck back. Think sports-tourer rather than sportsbike. It seemed to handle well, but it was shod with Maxxis SP tyres, and I could not bring myself to see how they dealt with me at Max Stupid. I’m funny about tyres. Most people are. There are brands you like and trust and there are brands you don’t. I have had nothing to do with Maxxis. I read good things about them, but the Internet is full of lies. Ridden at a few degrees less than Max Stupid, they seemed fine. I left it at that. The SR-S tipped in sweetly and held its line – and crucially, it did not lash out viciously when you gassed it on hard. Yes, this was certainly no GSX-R750. It didn’t seem to be strangled performance-wise. It just wasn’t angry. Looking at the numbers, it made sense. The CF‑Moto SR‑S750 makes 110 hp with 80 Nm of torque and weighs 213 kg, while the Suzuki GSX‑R750 makes 148 hp, has 86.3 Nm and weighs 190 kg. The wheelbase and rake comparisons are also revealing. The SR-S is 1419mm long and the GSX-R is 1390mm long. Their respective rakes are 24.5 degrees and 24.6 degrees. That there should tell you everything you need to know about why it’s not a GSX-R750. The SR-S is a slower-steering, slightly pudgier, and markedly less powerful bike than the legendary GSX-R750. But then it’s not trying to be one of those. Those days are gone. The people who wanted those numbers, or told themselves they did, are no more. The SRE-S is very much an in-line four 750 for our time. It is as modern as drone warfare. There is no key. There is no fob. There is a small black plastic thing a third the size of a credit card with which you touch a place on the inside left of the fairing. Then all its lights come on in a celebration of electric modernity. I hated that wee plastic thingy. I am guaranteed to lose such a starting gimmick. I hate fobs too. They solved a problem no-one was having. I can spend three days riding through rivers, jumping into oceans, and being rained on, and my bike key will still start my bike. My fob won’t. My key does not require batteries. My fob does. The SR-S750s starting “card” has no battery, and it may well work if I leave it in the sink overnight, so it may be an improvement on the fob. But I am primitively confident that whatever sorcery makes it speak to the fairing will, at the worst possible time, cease to speak to the fairing. But young people will love it. Technology does not mortify them like it does me. And they will be pleased you can also lock and unlock the thing with a password, Bluetooth, or via the CFMOTO RIDE app. There is also a three-way electric lock that does your steering, seat, and petrol cap. Once all the lights come on and you start it and are greeted with that lovely deep engine hum, riding it is a doddle. And it’s so smooth, like Chinese silk. This is no small thing. In-line fours all had a certain amount of handlebar “buzz” in them. It used to be hand and mind-numbing, but it got better as time went by, and then only really bothered people up near red-line. The SR-S750 is amazingly almost vibe-free. Like I said, the ergos are not sportbike ergos, and it is fuelled beautifully by Bosch. It’s just not going to shoot you at the horizon like you might think it will, given its looks and aero bits. Displayed on social media, the SR-S copped some flak for its fairing-mounted wings. From old people, mainly. The same old people who criticise the aero on BMW’s S1000RR and Ducati’s Panigale and view it as pointless. Thing is, the aero on those bikes does work. But you really have to be going seriously fast for it to do so. The SR-S750 does not go that fast. Most riders don’t go that fast either. So, its aero is a styling thing. Happily, there is an enormous amount of suspension and braking integrity to the bike, and its suite of electronics is top-notch – cornering ABS, Traction Control, and a Tyre Pressure Monitoring system are standard. The suspension up the front is a set of fully adjustable KYB 43mm USD forks, and there’s a fully adjustable KYB monoshock on the rear bolted to a single-sided swingarm. The brakes are four-piston 320mm Brembos up front, and a 240mm twin-piston unit on the back. There is a 6.2-inch TFT dashboard, and you can spend quality screen-time wandering through its permutations and info displays. It has a slipper clutch, and a quickshifter, which mainly worked on the upshift for me, and it seemed a bit glitchy now and again. Sometimes it worked fine up and down. Sometimes only up. Sometimes not at all. I’m certain this was an anomaly and not anything your dealer couldn’t immediately sort should you get this issue. No-one I spoke to who had ridden an SR-S had this problem. Crucially, it didn’t feel or look cheaply made, and it was great to ride. It felt sorted and stable. There was no twitchiness on fast direction changes, and the engine made exactly the right in-line four noises when I got enthusiastic. And it didn’t make me feel fat, crippled, and slow, like a GSX-R750 always did. It’s way too friendly for that. Personally, I’m strangely pleased someone re-invented the in-line four 750. It was always, and still is, a very cool engine configuration. That it is wedged into a modern, and very sassy-looking bike with great brakes and suspension should be celebrated. And here’s the best bit. That this package costs a ridiculous $AU12,990 ride-away in Australia simply beggars belief. I’m going to give CFMoto a round of applause. You Americans can't get this one yet – CFMoto has an odd habit of releasing its bikes everywhere else first. There are no dates or prices available for the USA at this point, but hey, there's always the 675SS, which now sells for an equally outrageous US$7,499. + 879.09 + 288.65 + 28.00 + 1,922.00 + 4,617.00 + 879.09 + 288.65 + 288.65 + 28.00 + 28.00 + 1,922.00 Studds Accessories, the country’s largest two-wheeler helmet maker, has seen its stock decline about 29 per cent from its ₹585 IPO price in November 2025 to ₹413.40 (BSE). Its market capitalisation has shrunk from around ₹2,300 crore at the IPO to ₹1,627 crore. The stock’s fall has been sharper than the broader market’s 12.2 per cent decline and the roughly 7.5 per cent correction in the Nifty Auto index since its November 7 listing, though  there are some stocks (Subros, Motherson Wiring, Amara Raja Energy) in the select auto ancillary space that have fallen 25-35 per cent in the same period. While we had suggested subscribing to the Studds IPO with a three-to-five-year horizon, our premise was that the valuation of 33 times FY25 earnings per share left little room for disappointment but long-term growth prospects made it worth considering. The subsequent stock price weakness reflects both valuation correction and some earnings growth concerns. FY26-adjusted revenue grew 8.6 per cent, slower than the 10.4 per cent growth in FY25. Subsequently, a sharp rise in raw material prices, aggravated by geopolitical disruptions and higher wage costs squeezed margins. In Q1FY27, though topline grew 13.8 per cent, EBITDA declined 35 per cent and net profit tanked 39 per cent year on year. Delays in commissioning additional capacity (manufacturing facility – V) have added to the uncertainty. At 19.7 times trailing 12-month earnings (and 21.4x based on FY26 earnings), Studds’ valuations are reasonable. Premium helmets and exports are gaining ground, while the balance sheet remains decent. This positions the stock for margin and profit growth recovery. Historically, EBITDA margins for the company were in the 11-12 per cent range in FY22 and FY23, before climbing to the 17-19 per cent range in later years. Q1FY27 margin stood at 11.5 per cent due to factors explained earlier. Bloomberg consensus estimates FY27 earnings per share at ₹17.80, down nearly 15.2 per cent from FY26. This is estimated to be followed by a smart recovery of EPS to ₹26.25 in FY28. Thus, Studds’ valuation argument rests on the expected earnings rebound. Therefore, long-term investors should stagger purchases in small quantities rather than assume that the stock correction has fully priced in the risks. Also, given the current sentiment in equity markets and rising interest scenario, investors should aim for a bigger margin of safety than in previous market regimes. Studds manufactures two-wheeler helmets under the Studds and SMK brands, besides supplying helmets under private labels and selling riding accessories. Studds caters mainly to the mass and mid-market segments, while SMK targets premium customers. The company holds about 25 per cent share of India’s domestic helmet market. Its manufacturing operations are concentrated in Faridabad, Haryana. The company undertakes most production processes in-house. This helps control quality and manufacturing costs, although margins remain exposed to fluctuations in plastic-derived raw materials. Note, Studds’ key raw materials include ABS (acrylonitrile butadiene styrene), polycarbonate and EPS (expanded polystyrene), along with paints, fabrics, visors and packaging materials. Just to give you some perspective, the average styrene-based raw material price was around Rs 135 at the beginning of Q4 FY26, which increased at its peak to approximately Rs 225 in Q1 FY27. That’s almost a 65 per cent increase in prices. This was an exceptional movement in raw material prices over such a short period of time. Studds sold 81.3 lakh helmets and boxes in FY26, with production of 82.7 lakh units and capacity utilisation of about 89 per cent. It has over 360 distributors in India and exports to more than 70 countries. The company is expanding annual helmet and box capacity from about 95 lakh units to 1.25 crore units through its fifth manufacturing facility. The first phase will add 15 lakh units annually. Studds also plans to expand beyond helmets into riding jackets, Bluetooth communication systems and bicycle helmets. It has secured a manufacturing relationship with Decathlon for bicycle helmets. These products are still relatively small contributors, but could broaden its revenue base over time. The management said underlying demand was stable across its key markets, supported by two-wheeler ownership, premium motorcycles, adventure touring and greater safety awareness. Studds expects stronger regulatory enforcement and premiumisation to encourage a shift from unorganised, price-driven helmet sales towards branded, safety-focussed products. The most encouraging development is the increasing contribution from premium helmets and exports. SMK’s revenue share rose from 11.8 per cent in FY25 to 15.7 per cent in FY26, while exports increased from 16.75 per cent to 20.1 per cent. Both offer an avenue for growth beyond the domestic mass-market helmet business. SMK generates EBITDA margins roughly 10 percentage points higher than Studds, while SMK exports can earn margins of 30-35 per cent. A greater contribution from these businesses could support profitability as volumes expand. Studds is also establishing direct dealer operations in Italy, Germany and France, aimed at reducing dependence on distributors in these markets. Its Italian subsidiary is expected to improve delivery responsiveness and support European expansion, although profitability will take time. Underlying demand has remained resilient. Q1 FY27 helmet volumes grew 8.5 per cent despite price increases, while revenue rose 13.8 per cent. The management expects volume growth of about 8-10 per cent for FY27. The balance sheet provides further comfort. Bloomberg data show FY26 cash of ₹84.6 crore against borrowings of ₹8.2 crore. Operating cash flow was ₹91.2 crore, against net profit of ₹82.6 crore. The immediate concern is profitability. EBITDA margin contracted from 20.3 per cent in Q1 FY26 to 11.5 per cent in Q1 FY27, as raw material costs and wages rose sharply. The management attributed around six percentage points of margin pressure to materials and another two percentage points to manpower costs (a change in the minimum wages in Haryana from 1st of April). Studds has increased selling prices by about 9 per cent, but the benefit is being realised gradually across customers. Raw material prices have moderated from their peak, although higher wage costs are likely to persist. The management expects EBITDA margins of 14-15 per cent in Q2 FY27 and a return to an 18-20 per cent quarterly run rate by Q4. Capacity expansion also needs monitoring. The first phase of the fifth facility was initially expected in Q4 FY26. Following successive delays, commercial production is now expected by October-end 2026, subject to approvals. The European direct-dealer venture is another execution risk, with the management expecting losses during its first two years. At the current price of ₹413.4, Studds trades at 19.7 times trailing 12-month earnings. The valuation is attractive if the projected recovery materialises. Further delays, sustained input-cost pressure or weaker-than-expected volumes could undermine that assumption. Hence, accumulating on dips would be the right approach at this stage. (Photo by Andrew Burton/Getty Images) A new report by the Federal Reserve published Friday indicates the wealth gap between affluent Americans and nearly everyone else has widened since the COVID-19 pandemic. While the median family net worth rose 2%, to nearly $216,000, from 2022-2025, the median net worth of surveyed individuals under the age of 35 dropped 23% — to around $33,000 — during that time frame, according to the Fed’s 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances. Notably, the median net worth of those 75 or older climbed 37%, to around $504,900. (RELATED: It’s Harder For Zoomers To Afford These Five Mainstays Of Life That Boomers Could When They Were Their Age) The White House did not immediately respond to the Daily Caller News Foundation’s request for comment. The Fed told the DCNF that it didn’t have anything else to share beyond its report. Chart showing the 2025 Survey of Consumer Finance’s median net worth by age from 2022-2025. (Courtesy of the Federal Reserve)  Other age brackets, however, didn’t appear to fare much better. The median net worth of respondents between the ages of 45 and 54 and 65 to 74 fell 6% and 4%, respectively. That metric, on the other hand, rose among respondents between the ages of 35 and 44 and 55 to 64 by 5% and 3%, respectively. One factor which may have influenced these changes is participation in the stock market. Trading declined from 58% in 2022 to 56% in 2025, largely driven by lower participation of those outside of the top 10% of the income distribution identified in the report. The S&P 500 index, however, rose 78% from 2023 through 2025, The Motley Fool reported in January. The report follows a study conducted by crypto casino BC Game finding the median costs of used cars, college, housing, weddings, and childcare outpaced wage growth from 1985 through 2026. Both reports were released as Democrats and Republicans jockey over affordability ahead of the November midterm elections, when rising angst from younger generations concerning America’s current economic order may be prove to have a key effect on which party secures a majority in the next Congress. Support for capitalism among Americans under the age of 30 dropped from 52% to 48% since 2018, while support for socialism rose from 19% to 21%, according to a CBS News poll published Sept. 24. However, Public Opinion Strategies pollster Micah Roberts told the outlet that the apparent rise in support for the Democratic Socialists of America’s agenda is “really about frustration with the status quo.” TRENDING ©2026 The Daily Caller, Inc. It had been a while since Dyson had genuinely surprised us with a product launch, but then the brand unveiled its first toothbrush. Dyson is already a familiar name in personal care, thanks to its now well established hair-styling gadgets, so a move into oral care wasn't entirely left-field. Still, when the CameraJet made its debut, it was still quite the swerve – taking Dyson from the dressing table to the bathroom sink. The first product has to be radically different... otherwise we wouldn't consider it When I caught up with Jake Dyson — son of founder, James, and Dyson's chief engineer — at the brand's Unveiled event, I wanted to know what prompted such a move. And, more broadly, how a brand might end up with such a twisty, turny product roadmap. (For clarity, throughout this article I'll be using "Dyson" to mean the brand, and "Jake" to mean the person.) So, if a toothbrush can become a Dyson gadget, is there anything that couldn't be? "No, it doesn't," Jake declares. "It has to be radically different." He expands: "The first product has to be radically different, and have performance claims, and a difference against a competitor by a magnitude; otherwise, we wouldn't consider it."      In short, the brand isn't interested in having a go at anything; it wants to make a splash in markets that have grown stagnant. The launch of the first Dyson Supersonic hair dryer in 2016 is a great example — it blew new life into a market that had barely seen change in decades. And the CameraJet is far from your average toothbrush. It's kitted out with a camera that will stream a live view of the inside of your mouth back to you, and is trained to recognize gaps in your teeth and shoot water/mouthwash at them, to take care of flossing. Whether or not it enjoys the success of the Supersonic remains to be seen, but it certainly checks that "radically different" box. "It's got to work properly," asserts Jake. "I mean, we probably could have launched [the CameraJet] two years ago, but it wouldn't have hit every gap perfectly, and that's not acceptable." President Donald Trump announced Friday that Russia has agreed to supply millions of tons of diesel fuel to the American and global market, following a call with Russian President Vladimir Putin. The president said the first shipments would begin immediately, with larger deliveries scheduled through November and beyond in a post on Truth Social. Trump laid out a delivery schedule that escalates over time: I have just concluded a highly successful discussion with President Vladimir Putin, of Russia, wherein it was agreed that Russia will immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace, another 500,000 Tons during the month of November, and 1,000,000 Tons immediately thereafter. The president said Russia would then deliver up to 3,000,000 additional tons, depending on the condition of its refineries. He tied the arrangement to U.S. leverage in the Persian Gulf, where American forces have operated throughout the war with Iran. “Between our TOTAL CONTROL of the Strait of Hormuz, and this great announcement on Russian Energy, Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!” Trump wrote. Trump named lower prices for American farmers, ranchers, and truckers as his priority and closed the announcement with a line on Tehran. “Iran will not have a Nuclear Weapon!” Trump added. The announcement follows the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which the president signed into law last month. The statute takes effect Oct. 19, directs tariffs of up to 500 percent on Russian goods, and allows secondary sanctions on countries that purchase Russian fuel. Many of the law’s provisions can be waived by the president. Trump imposed major oil sanctions on Russia last October but issued waivers this year, citing disruptions from the Iran conflict that drove up energy costs and inflation. The deal lands as diesel sits near a record of roughly $6.50 a gallon weeks before the November midterms. Last week, Trump said Europe had agreed to release diesel reserves “immediately,” and days later he signed an order expanding access to tax-exempt red-dyed diesel at a rally in Nebraska.
